Atlas: Filing your 83(b) election using Auto 83(b)

This article describes how Atlas automatically files 83(b) tax elections for C-corp founders (included in the initial Atlas incorporation fee). This article was last updated in September 2024.

What is an 83(b) tax election?

The section 83(b) election lets the IRS know that you’d like to be taxed on your equity on the date the equity was granted to you rather than on the date the equity vests. If you are currently a US taxpayer or plan to become one in the future while your equity is vesting, this filing could save you a significant amount on future taxes. Each founder must file their own 83(b) tax election.

83(b) elections must be filed within 30 calendar days of when each founder purchases their shares in the company. 83(b) election filings are considered on time if they are postmarked - in other words, when the United States Postal Service first makes a record that they received the letter and generates tracking information. The postmark date is sufficient to consider the filing “on time”, even if it’s not delivered to the IRS by the 30 day deadline.

Atlas files 83(b) elections for all C-corp founders

For accounts created after July 2024, Atlas now files 83(b) elections for all C-corp founders. LLC founders do not need to file an 83(b) tax election, as equity in an LLC created with Atlas does not vest.

Do I need an SSN or ITIN to file an 83(b) election?

No. Though the 83(b) election requires that each founder provides a Social Security Number (SSN) or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) if they have one, you can file an 83(b) election even if you do not have a US tax ID.

If you have an SSN or ITIN, we’ll pre-fill this on your 83(b) election form. If you don’t have either type of tax ID, Atlas will still file an 83(b) election for you, so that in the event you become a US taxpayer during the vesting period, you are covered. If you plan to become a US taxpayer in the future, you can still file this election when you incorporate with Atlas and apply for an ITIN later. You do not need to provide an ITIN to file an 83(b) election.

Founders who wish not to file an 83(b) election should not use Atlas to incorporate.

How does Atlas file 83(b) elections?

  • Atlas collects permission to file an 83(b) tax election on behalf of founders, and founders’ signatures for the 83(b) tax election itself, during the Atlas application . Founders can file using Atlas whether or not they have a US taxpayer ID (SSN or ITIN).
  • Atlas will automatically file an 83(b) election via USPS Certified Mail after your company is incorporated and each founder’s share purchase is complete.
  • You’ll receive email updates when your election has been filed and when it arrives at the IRS. Atlas will provide you with a proof of filing document, which includes relevant details such as filing date and tracking events from USPS. A copy of your signed 83(b) election and proof of filing will always be available in your Atlas dashboard.
  • You should screenshot the official USPS tracking page showing that your letter was postmarked before your filing deadline. You can access the tracking page with the tracking number we provide. Your 83(b) election is considered filed when it is postmarked. It does not have to be delivered to be successfully filed with the IRS.

When will Atlas file my 83(b) election?

Your 83(b) election will be filed within 10 business days of your share purchase (which happens right after you incorporate), well before the 30 day deadline for filing.

Once USPS has received your filing, you’ll receive a USPS tracking number. We’ll email you with important updates, and you can track your filing’s progress in the Atlas dashboard or on the official USPS website.

The 83(b) election deadline is calculated based on when your letter is postmarked (ie. mailed), so no need to worry about when it is delivered.

Screenshotting your proof of filing

In addition to the proof of 83(b) election filing provided by Atlas, tax experts suggest taking a screenshot of the official USPS tracking information to prove that your 83(b) election was filed on time. In the unexpected case of an IRS audit, you can use both the 83(b) proof of filing and the screenshot as evidence that you filed your 83(b) election on time. Make sure it includes your tracking number, and the ‘Accepted at USPS Regional Origin Facility’ status.

It’s important to take your screenshot soon after your 83(b) election is postmarked, because the USPS only retains tracking details for 2 years. Your proof of filing document provided by Atlas will always be available in the Atlas dashboard. Users will now see this screenshot task in the “What’s Next?” section of their Dashboard after they receive their EIN.

Does my spouse need to sign my 83(b) election?

If you live in a community property state (AZ, CA, ID, LA, NV, NM, TX, WA, WI), we suggest you inform your spouse about your 83(b) election filing. Treasury regulations don’t require a spousal signature for a valid 83(b) election, and your election is valid without it. However, if you and your spouse disagree over the tax treatment of your shares, you could be responsible for your spouse’s lack of knowledge about the election. As always, consult a tax professional for advice specific to your situation.

Atlas: Purchasing stock with IP - FAQ

What is IP?

IP, or Intellectual Property, is a creation owned by an individual or company that is protected by law, similar to how physical property such as real estate is protected. The most common forms of IP are copyrights, trademarks, patents, and trade secrets.

As you start working on your company, you are likely developing multiple forms of IP: business plans and strategies, product prototypes, software code, domain names, logos, websites, sketches, drawings, algorithms, company processes, customer lists, and “negative know-how” (things you’ve learned not to do). It is not necessary to have registered your IP (i.e., patent filings, trademark filings, domain names, etc.) for it to be protected. If you have been developing the business model or product for your new company, you likely have created IP.

How do I use my IP to purchase my shares?

When incorporating your business, it is essential that you purchase your shares from the corporation. You can do so using cash or IP. Atlas makes it easy to use IP – you can click a button in our dashboard and use the IP that you are already contributing to the business during the incorporation process to purchase your shares. If you have developed significant company-related IP, like patents worth substantially more than $100, Atlas might not be right for you.

How much do I need to pay for my shares? How does this work if I’m using IP?

Your company will have 10,000,000 authorized shares and fair market value (FMV) of $100 (this is industry standard). Atlas follows the standard market practice of assuming that at formation, your company is worth US$0.00001 multiplied by the number of issued shares; this totals $100. You need to purchase your shares at par value (US $0.00001 each). Atlas calculates the amount you need to pay, in either cash or with IP, to purchase your shares. For example, if you own 85.0% of the company, which is 8,500,000 shares and each share is initially worth US$0.00001, the purchase price of your shares is US$85.00.

Because the amount you will pay for your shares is small, newly formed companies generally assume that your existing IP is worth at least the value of the shares you are purchasing from the company. Using Atlas ensures that your contribution qualifies as a tax free exchange. If you believe that you hold IP that is worth substantially more than your shares, please seek the advice of an attorney or tax accountant.

Why should I contribute my IP to the company?

You need to contribute your IP to the company because the company must own the IP it uses to operate. When you create a company using Atlas, all founders assign relevant IP —both IP that is developed prior to forming your company as well as the IP that will be developed after the company is formed—to the company. Future investors and potential acquirers will expect that your company owns this IP when entering into an agreement with you, and assigning your IP to your company could help you avoid future litigation over IP ownership, for example if a founder were to leave the company.

Transferring your IP at the time you form your company also avoids negative tax implications.

Is there any IP that I should not be contributing to the company?

You should only contribute IP relevant to your newly formed company. In Atlas, unrelated IP from things like side projects, previous startups, or personal inventions are not assigned to your company upon incorporation. Similarly, employers—both prior and current—usually own the IP you created while working for them. You cannot use this IP in your new business and, because you don’t own it, you cannot assign it to your new business. The legal documents you sign while incorporating a business with Atlas contribute only your IP that relates to the company. Read more from Cooley about Moonlighting

This FAQ is not intended to be legal or tax advice. Circumstances will vary substantially. Atlas provides documentation and incorporation services only. We are happy to refer you to qualified legal, tax and accounting professionals if you have any questions.

What documentation can I use to demonstrate that I purchased my shares with IP?

Your Confidential Information and Inventions Assignment Agreement (CIIAA) assigns all company-related IP you create to the company you are forming. When you purchase with IP, Exhibit B to the Common Stock Purchase Agreement (CSPA) is an Assignment of IP and Other Assets and contains the terms of the IP assignment used to purchase your shares. Both the CIIAA and CSPA can be found on your Atlas Documents page.

Cancel Stripe Atlas incorporation

If you have signed your company formation documents, we can’t cancel your company’s formation. If you do not intend to operate your company, you will need to dissolve your company to avoid any ongoing obligations such as taxes. Closing your Stripe Atlas account does not dissolve your company.

Stripe Atlas works with Soxton, an online legal services firm, to connect Stripe Atlas users with lawyers who can help with company dissolutions. Schedule a consultation with Soxton to discuss your options. Once you have finalized the dissolution, download your formation documents from the company section of your Stripe dashboard, and close your Stripe account.

Choosing a Name for Your Stripe Atlas Company

To prevent delays, you’ll need to confirm that your preferred company name is available and that it’s not already taken by another entity in Delaware.

To confirm this in a minute or less, you can search Delaware’s name database, following the below instructions depending on your entity type.

C Corporation

  • Select “Corporation” from “Entity Kind”
  • Select “INC.” from “Entity Ending”
  • Enter your preferred company name
    • There’s no need to enter the entity suffix in this box. For example, if you’d like your company to be called Testing, Inc., you’ll enter Testing into this box.
  • Search for your company name

LLC

  • Select “Limited Liability Company (LLC)” from “Entity Kind”
  • Select “LLC” from “Entity Ending”
  • Enter your preferred company name
    • There’s no need to enter the suffix in this box. For example, if you’d like your company to be called Testing, LLC, you’ll enter Testing into this box.
  • Search your company name

If your preferred name is available, you’ll be re-directed to a page to reserve your name. You are not required to reserve your name at this point. A re-direct to this page is simply confirmation that your preferred name is available in Delaware.

If your name’s already taken in Delaware, a message will appear below the search button. It will read: “The name is not available for reservation”. Unfortunately, you’ll need to select a different name.

If you have any questions about choosing your Stripe Atlas company name, please reach out to atlas@stripe.com.

Closing your Stripe Atlas account

Closing your Stripe payments account doesn’t close or dissolve your Stripe Atlas company with Delaware.

If you are planning to continue operating your company but would like to close your Stripe account, please take the following steps:

  • Migrate your registered agent service: When you close your Stripe account, we cancel your registered agent subscription on your behalf so you are not charged upon renewal. However, all Delaware companies are required to maintain a registered agent. If you would like to renew your service, you can follow up with LegalInc (or any other provider of your choice), but we will not be able to renew your subscription moving forward. You can contact Legalinc at atlas-support@legalinc.com. If you plan to change your registered agent please report this to the State of Delaware.

If you plan to close your Stripe account and no longer operate the company, please take the following steps:

  • Dissolve your company: Even if you are not operating your company anymore, you may still be obligated to file taxes every year until it’s dissolved. A final tax filing may also be required for the year in which your company dissolves. It’s a good idea to work with an accountant to confirm your tax obligations. Atlas partners with three solutions, but you can use any service you’d like:
  • Soxton, an online legal services firm, connects Stripe Atlas users with lawyers who can help with company dissolutions. Reach out for a free, 15 minute consultation. They offer $300 dissolution plus guidance on how to pay any outstanding taxes owed.
  • Legalinc, the provider of Atlas company’s registered agent services, offers $99 dissolution plus guidance on how to pay any outstanding taxes owed.
  • SimpleClosure helps founders shut down quickly and confidently through a tech-enabled and expert-led process. Their in-house team handles the heavy lifting, and founders can begin dissolving in <24 hours. Atlas founders receive 10% off.
  • Download your formation documents from the company section of your Stripe dashboard.
  • Contact your bank to close your bank account.
  • Close your Stripe account. When you close your Stripe account we cancel your registered agent subscription on your behalf so you are not charged upon renewal.

If you have any questions, don’t hesitate to reach out to atlas@stripe.com.

Dissolving your company

Even if you are not operating your company anymore, you may still be obligated to file taxes every year until it’s dissolved. A final tax filing may also be required for the year in which your company dissolves. It’s a good idea to work with an accountant to confirm your tax obligations.

  • Choose a service to help you dissolve your company. Atlas partners with three solutions, but you can use any service you’d like:
    • SimpleClosure helps founders shut down quickly and confidently through a tech-enabled and expert-led process. Their in-house team handles the heavy lifting, and founders can begin dissolving in <24 hours. Atlas founders receive 10% off.
    • Soxton, an online legal services firm, connects Stripe Atlas users with lawyers who can help with company dissolutions. $300 dissolution plus guidance on how to pay any outstanding taxes owed.
    • Legalinc, the registered agent for Atlas companies, offers $99 dissolution plus guidance on how to pay any outstanding taxes owed.
  • Download your formation documents from the company section of your Stripe dashboard.
  • Contact your bank to close your bank account.
  • Close your Stripe account. When you close your Stripe account we cancel your registered agent subscription on your behalf so you are not charged upon renewal.
  • You can also cancel your registered agent subscription from the Dashboard without closing your account.
  • If you dissolved your company via Legalinc, Atlas will automatically cancel your registered agent subscription once the dissolution is complete.

FAQ for Indian Founders using Stripe Atlas

Indian founders can use Atlas to incorporate a US company, access $2,500 in Stripe product credits, and receive over $50K of partner discounts and credits. Read our Indian Founder Guide for step-by-step guidance. This article was updated in August 2025.

Complying with Indian ODI regulations

If I live in India, can I use Atlas to incorporate a US company while complying with India’s ODI regulations?

Yes. If you live in India, you can incorporate a company using Stripe Atlas and comply with the Reserve Bank of India’s overseas direct investment (ODI) regulations.

To learn more about how to use Atlas compliantly, follow our detailed Indian Founder Guide to incorporate a US C Corp using Atlas.

Are payments to Atlas compliant with India’s ODI regulations?

Yes. Atlas charges 500 USD to generate, execute, and file documents for founders. This Atlas service is not a foreign investment subject to ODI regulations.

You can pay Atlas using a credit or debit card under the LRS, which permits up to $250K USD to be remitted abroad each year by each Indian resident.

What are my ongoing reporting requirements in India once my US entity is incorporated?

Indian founders with US entities need to complete two filings each year.

First, an Annual Performance Report (APR) with respect to any US entity, with your Authorised Dealer Bank (AD Bank), on an annual basis by 31st December. Note that only the founder with the largest equity stake is required to file. If equity is equally distributed, a joint filing is acceptable.

Second, file Form FLA regarding the overseas investments made by an Indian entity, with the Reserve Bank of India, on an annual basis by July 15th of every year.

Our Indian compliance partner, Inkle, can help with both of these filings. Contact them at incorporate@inkle.io.

What documents do authorised dealer (AD) banks normally need for ODI transactions?

Founders should consult their AD bank for specifics. Applications usually include each LLP’s agreement, PAN card, certificate of incorporation, and stock purchase resolution. They should also include the US subsidiary’s certificate of incorporation, stock purchase agreement, and a signed Form FC and the bank’s version of Form A2.

Setting Up Your Business Structure

Why is it more common to form an Indian Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) than a Private Limited Company (Pvt Ltd) as a parent for the US C corp?

LLPs involve lesser administrative burdens and costs than Private Limited Companies. While LLPs can’t issue equity, that isn’t a problem: investors will purchase equity in the US C Corp and Indian employees usually receive stock from the Indian Pvt Ltd subsidiary.

Why can’t co-founders jointly own a single Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) or Private Limited Company (Pvt Ltd) to own their US C corp equity?

Creating an LLP for each founder is common practice to simplify equity vesting agreements. When each founder has their own LLP, that LLP can sign a vesting agreement directly with the US C corp. If the founders instead use a joint LLP or Pvt Ltd, the C corp would sign a vesting agreement with the joint LLP or Pvt Ltd, and each founder would then need to sign an additional vesting agreement with the LLP or Pvt Ltd.

Why do Indian founders commonly set up a Private Limited Company as a subsidiary for their US C corp?

If founders want to operate in India (which includes one or more founders residing in India), they should consider creating an Indian Private Limited Company subsidiary for their US C corp. Creating an Indian subsidiary helps Indian startups more easily collect GST, employ people in India, and access tax benefits. Founders living in India are typically employed by the Private Limited Company subsidiary.

Unlike LLPs, private limited companies can issue equity and manage Indian employee ESOPs.

How should I create an Indian Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) or Private Limited Company (Pvt Ltd)?

Inkle has published an overview of the process to form an Indian LLP and Private Limited Company. We encourage Indian founders to email Inkle at incorporate@inkle.io if they’d like support forming either of those Indian entities.

What should my LLP resolution to purchase my US C corp’s stock include?

Resolutions should include a brief addendum explaining the purpose of the investment, that it is a bona fide business (i.e., one that is legal in both India and the US), and that the US C corp’s $100 valuation is due to the C corp having just formed.

Atlas developed a template LLP resolution with JSA, a major Indian law firm with a dedicated startup practice. Simply fill out and sign the template for it to be legally effective. If you have questions about filling out the template, please consult an Indian lawyer.

Using Stripe Atlas

Will Atlas file my 83(b) election?

Atlas does not file Section 83(b) elections for subsidiaries, but provides instructions and a template for Indian founders to do so themselves. The template can also be used by non-Indian founders.

Generally, startup lawyers recommend founders outside the US who file US tax returns or think they might become a US taxpayer in future make an 83(b) election because it might reduce their future US tax liability. If a founder isn’t currently a US taxpayer and doesn’t anticipate becoming one in the future, they don’t need to make an 83(b) election because it affects only US tax liability.

What if I submitted an Atlas application for a standard (i.e., non-subsidiary) C corp and discovered afterward I needed to form a subsidiary instead?

In these situations, we recommend founding teams cancel their Atlas application and begin a new one, following the steps in our Indian Founder Guide.

To do so, founders should reach out to Atlas support via the Stripe dashboard, and let support know they’d like to cancel their Atlas application and receive a refund because one or more of the founders is an Indian resident.

Are there any separate steps for non-Indian residents who are founding a startup with Indian residents?

To ensure Indian founders are compliant with ODI laws, we advise teams with Indian and non-Indian founders to choose the “Subsidiary” structure in the Atlas application.

Non-Indian founders should purchase their US C corp stock using a standard Restricted Stock Purchase Agreement, rather than the template that Atlas provides for Indian founders. We encourage non-Indian founders to utilize CooleyGo’s free Delaware C corp document generator to do so.

Does Atlas provide a Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreement (CIIAA)?

For subsidiaries, Atlas doesn’t automatically generate a CIIAA for founders. We encourage teams with Indian resident founders to generate and execute a CIIAA template using CooleyGo’s free Delaware C corp document generator.

Form a US C Corporation or a Limited Liability Company with Stripe Atlas

Stripe Atlas supports two options for forming a US company in Delaware:

  • C Corporation
  • Limited Liability Company (LLC)

Due to the differences between them, an entity type that works for one founder may not work for another. There are a number of factors that you’ll need to consider when deciding on which entity type to choose, including your plans for funding, taxes, and ownership structure. For more information see: LLCs vs. C corporations.

Stripe Atlas cannot offer specific advice on which legal entity type is best for you. If you would like to seek legal counsel for help, Soxton is an online legal services firm offering fixed fee packages. Learn more about Soxton.

If you’re looking to start an LLC outside Delaware, Stripe recommends that you consider doola. doola supports LLC formation in all 50 states, with deep support for international founders starting a US business. They also offer EIN support, business bank account guidance, bookkeeping, business tax filings, and ongoing compliance support. Get started with doola.

Contact us with any other questions: atlas@stripe.com. We’re here to help!

Founder equity terms

Learn about selecting your equity vesting terms.

Atlas defaults to industry-standard founder equity vesting terms. However, you can customize your vesting period and vesting start dates, and choose whether to include a vesting cliff.

Standard equity terms

As a founder, you need to understand the following equity terms:

  • Vesting: The process by which you gradually gain ownership of assets such as company equity over time, rather than receiving them all at once.
  • Vesting period: The total length of time over which you earn your founder equity. If you leave before the end of the vesting period, you only keep the stock that has already vested.
  • Vesting cliffs: The date before which no equity vests. If you leave before the cliff date, you won’t receive any stock.
  • Vesting start date: The date when your vesting period begins.

Most founders set up their companies with a four year vesting period and a one year cliff, with a vesting start date set as the date of incorporation. All Atlas founder equity vests monthly. For example, with a four year vesting period, founders receive 1/48 of their total grant each month.

Here’s what these standard terms mean for your startup:

  • Four year vesting period: Your founder equity vests in monthly increments over four years.
  • One year cliff: No equity vests until you have been with the company for a full year. With a four year vesting period, 25% of shares vest immediately on the cliff date.
  • Vesting start date as day of incorporation: Vesting begins the day your company is incorporated.

Select your equity terms

As a C Corp founder, you can select equity vesting terms that differ from the industry standard.

You can select your equity terms for your founding team in the Atlas application:

  • In your Atlas application in the Dashboard, navigate to the Equity terms page.
  • Select the equity vesting period for your entire founding team.
  • For each founder, choose between a one year cliff or no cliff. However, a one-year cliff is typically the industry standard and preferred by investors.
  • Select a vesting start date up to 6 months before the current date for each founder.
  • Review selections on the application summary page before you submit your application.
Equity terms selection

The founder who submits your Atlas application selects the equity terms for all team members. We recommend that your team discusses your desired equity terms before submitting the application.

Vesting period

The vesting period determines how long it takes for your founder equity to vest in full. Atlas allows you to select a vesting period that applies to all founders of the company:

  • 4 years (default)
  • 5 years
  • 6 years

You might extend the vesting period to increase founder retention and signal long-term commitment to investors, especially in industries with longer development timelines.

Vesting cliff

A vesting cliff is an initial period during which no shares vest.

You can use Atlas to customize vesting cliffs for each founder:

  • One-year cliff (default): You must stay for one year before any shares vest. For example, in a four-year vesting schedule, after this initial one-year period, 25% of shares vest immediately, with the remainder vesting monthly.
  • No cliff: Shares begin vesting immediately according to the monthly vesting schedule, without a waiting period.

Founders might remove the cliff because the team wants to be rewarded for their work regardless of how long they remain with the startup. However, a one-year cliff is the industry standard and is generally preferred by investors.

Vesting start date

The vesting start date determines when your vesting period begins.

You can use Atlas to customize the vesting start date for each founder:

  • The date of incorporation (default)
  • Up to 6 months before the date of incorporation

You might set a vesting start date prior to incorporation to acknowledge work completed for the startup before it was officially incorporated.

Limitations

Atlas doesn’t support equity customization beyond the options listed above. For questions and feedback on customizations, contact us at atlas-feedback@stripe.com.

Fundraising with SAFEs FAQ

Stripe users with an eligible US C corporation can fundraise using Simple Agreements for Future Equity (SAFEs). Founders can create, send, and track their SAFEs from the Fundraising tab in their Dashboard. Read about sending a SAFE with Stripe.

SAFEs overview

What are SAFEs?

Simple Agreements for Future Equity (SAFEs) allow you to raise money from investors by giving them the right to receive equity in your company when you later raise your first priced round or have a liquidity event. The SAFE was developed by Y Combinator in 2013 and has since become a common way for early-stage companies to raise money.

What are the different types of SAFEs?

There are multiple types of SAFEs. Three commonly used types are:

  • Valuation cap: Sets a maximum company valuation at which the SAFE converts into equity. According to data from Carta, this is the most used type of SAFE.
    • Example: You raise a 100,000 USD SAFE with a 5M USD valuation cap, and your next round is priced at 10M USD. The SAFE converts as if your company were valued at 5M USD, with the investor getting 100,000 USD/5,000,000 USD = 2% of your company rather than 100,000 USD/10,000,000 USD = 1% of your company.
  • Discount: Gives your investor a percentage discount on the price per share in your next priced round when their SAFE converts to equity.
    • Example: You raise a 100,000 USD SAFE with a 20% discount. When the next round prices shares at 1.00 USD each, the investor’s shares convert at 0.80 USD per share (1.00 USD*(1-20%)), so the investor gets 100,000 USD/0.80 USD = 125,000 shares rather than 100,000 USD/1.00 USD = 100,000 shares.
  • Valuation cap + discount: Sets a maximum company valuation at which the SAFE converts into equity and gives your investor a discount on the price per share in your next priced round. The SAFE converts at whichever gives the investor the most equity in your business: the valuation cap or the discount.
    • Example: You raise a 100,000 USD SAFE with a 5M USD cap and a 20% discount. Your next round is priced at 10M USD and your shares are priced at 1.00 USD. The SAFE converts based on the 5M USD cap because it gives them more shares than the 20% discount.
      • Discount calculation:
        • 20% discount on 1.00 USD = 0.80 USD
        • 100,000 USD/0.80 USD = 125,000 shares
      • Valuation cap calculation:
        • Share price at 5M USD cap = 5,000,000 USD/10,000,000 USD = 0.50 USD
        • 100,000 USD/0.50 USD = 200,000 shares
How does a valuation cap work?

A valuation cap is the maximum company valuation at which the SAFE converts into equity in your company.

If your next priced round gives your company a higher valuation than the valuation cap of a SAFE, the SAFE investor receives shares in your company as if the company were valued at the valuation cap rather than the new, higher valuation. Their ownership will be calculated as their investment divided by the valuation cap, rather than their investment divided by the new valuation. This results in them getting a larger share of your company equity than they would if they did not have a valuation cap.

If you raise money at a lower valuation than the valuation cap of a SAFE, the investor on that SAFE receives shares based on the new company valuation, rather than the valuation cap.

Do investors need to be accredited?

Lawyers recommend that SAFE investors are accredited. Raising from non-accredited investors is technically possible under certain exemptions, but it adds legal and administrative complexity, including detailed disclosure requirements and compliance with securities laws.

For most early-stage startups, leading law firms for startups like Cooley advise that costs and risks of raising from non-accredited investors outweigh the benefits.

Board consent

Why does my board need to sign a board consent?

A company’s board of directors should authorize any fundraising, including SAFEs. Board consent is the formal record of your board’s approval. It ensures your company follows standard corporate governance procedures.

What do I do if I want to raise more than my board consent allows?

A board consent authorizes a specific amount of fundraising with SAFEs. If you try to raise more than what was approved, you’ll need to work with an attorney to update the fundraising maximum in your board consent. If you are setting up the board consent in Stripe, set a maximum raise amount that is higher than what you anticipate you’ll need to fundraise, giving yourself a buffer in case you later decide to raise more and avoiding the need to work with an attorney.

Can I obtain board consent in retrospect after collecting funds?

Lawyers recommend obtaining board authorization prior to fundraising.

Fundraising with SAFEs

Who can use SAFEs?

Eligible US C corporations can use SAFEs.

To check your company’s eligibility, open the Fundraising tab in your Dashboard.

Does a Stripe board consent cover past SAFE fundraising?

No, the Stripe-generated board consent document only covers future fundraising. If you want to secure board consent for fundraising that has already taken place off Stripe, consult a lawyer.

Do Stripe SAFEs support SAFEs with valuation caps and discounts?

Stripe supports SAFEs with either a valuation cap or a discount. Stripe doesn’t support SAFEs that combine both a valuation cap and a discount.

Who created the SAFE template offered by Stripe?

Stripe SAFEs use the industry-trusted post-money Y Combinator (YC) template.

“Post-money” means the SAFE investor’s ownership is calculated as a percentage of the company after their SAFE and all other issued SAFEs have converted, and the investment is included in the company valuation used for this calculation. For instance, if you raise a 500,000 USD SAFE on a 5M USD post-money valuation, your investor will own 10% of the company after conversion.

Can I send a SAFE to individual and institutional investors, like VCs?

Yes. You can send Stripe SAFEs to individuals and institutional investors.

How do I correct a mistake in a SAFE, like an incorrect name or investment amount?

If you discover a mistake in a SAFE that you’ve already sent to an investor, you can void it from your Dashboard:

  • In your Dashboard, go to the Fundraising tab, find the SAFE you’d like to void, click the three dots in its row, and select Void. The SAFE’s status will update to Voided.
  • The company signer and investor will receive an email from “Stripe via DocuSign” notifying them that the SAFE has been voided.
  • After voiding the SAFE, you can create a new one by clicking Create SAFE in your Fundraising tab.

What happens after both parties sign the SAFE?

If you have a Stripe business account (Treasury onboarded): Stripe automatically emails the investor a link to an investment details page. You also receive a confirmation that the funding request was sent.

If you don’t have a Stripe business account: Stripe notifies you that both parties have signed. You’ll need to share your bank details with the investor directly and coordinate the transfer outside of Stripe.

What is the investment details page? (Treasury accounts only)

If you have a Stripe business account, the investment details page shows your investor:

  • The commitment amount
  • The investment name and current status
  • Your company’s Stripe business account routing and account number, or wallet address, depending on your currency eligibility

The investor copies these details to send funds from their bank account or custodial wallet. They can transfer the full commitment or a partial amount.

How does receiving funds affect my SAFE status?

If you have a Stripe business account: When funds arrive they appear in your Balances and the SAFE automatically updates to Funded in the Fundraising table — no manual step is required.

If you don’t have a Stripe business account: After you confirm receipt of funds through your external bank, go to the Fundraising table and manually mark the SAFE as Funded.

What funding methods are available? (Treasury accounts only)

If you have a Stripe business account, the following methods can be used to fund your SAFE:

  • Stripe doesn’t support SWIFT transfers for funding SAFEs.
  • If you have a business account that supports either fiat (USD) and/or stablecoin (USDC), then the investor details page will include account and wallet info respectively.

How do I receive funds without a Stripe business account?

Share your bank account details directly with the investor. Once funds have been received, open the Fundraising table in your Dashboard and manually update the SAFE status to Funded.

Legal notice

This article is for informational purposes only and is not legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel regarding SAFE terms, SEC accredited-investor requirements, and any other applicable laws or regulations.

Do I need a lawyer to fundraise with a SAFE using Stripe?

Stripe Fundraising is designed to be used without help from a lawyer, but you can always consult one if you have additional questions.

Can I fundraise with Stripe if I didn’t incorporate my company using Atlas?

Yes, eligible US C corporations can use Stripe to fundraise.

How can I forward my mail to my company address outside of the U.S.?

If you are looking for an address to receive mail, we would recommend using a mail forwarding service. Atlas users can access discounts at two providers:

  • Stable offers Stripe Atlas users 3 months free via a link in the Atlas application.
  • LegalZoom Virtual Mail offers Stripe Atlas users a 30% discount.

Your registered agent in Delaware will receive official government notices and act as a liaison between your company and the state. It is solely an address for your company to receive legal notices and communications from the government (from the State of Delaware for example) and to receive notice of any legal claims against your company in the unfortunate event that your company faces a lawsuit.

Your first year of registered agent services is included in your one-time Stripe Atlas fee. The renewal fee is $100, and it will be charged to your credit card on file each year.

How can I let Stripe Atlas know I’ve reserved my company name?

If you’ve already reserved your preferred company name with the State of Delaware, the name will no longer show as available on the website during the reservation period. In order to submit formation documents to Delaware, Stripe Atlas will need to provide a copy of the payment receipt.

You can send us a copy of the receipt with the subject line “Company name reservation receipt” to atlas@stripe.com. Providing this receipt before we submit your documents to Delaware will help prevent your company incorporation from being delayed.

How to check your EIN status with the IRS

To retrieve your EIN from the IRS, Atlas account openers should retrieve your company’s SS-4 form from the Documents tab of your Dashboard and have it available when you call the IRS at (+1) 800-829-4933. There is currently no way to check EIN status online.

Overview

As part of forming your company using Stripe Atlas, you’ll complete a Form SS-4, which we send to the IRS to request an EIN for your new company. If the account opener for the company provides a US Social Security Number (SSN), US company address, and US phone number, Stripe Atlas can request an EIN for the company through an online expedited process. For all other users, the IRS can take several weeks to assign your EIN. Stripe Atlas will call the IRS to retrieve the EIN as quickly as possible, and we will email you when it’s available in your Dashboard. The IRS typically mails a physical copy of your EIN letter to your company address in about 8 weeks.

Do I need my EIN to open a bank account and accept payments through my company?

If you incorporated with Stripe Atlas, you can bank and accept payments prior to receiving your EIN.

  • Banking: You’ll be able to open a bank account with one of Atlas’ banking partners listed in your Atlas dashboard prior to receiving your EIN. You’ll still need to provide it to those partners within 60 days.
  • Payments: You’ll be able to accept Stripe payments before receiving your EIN, although you won’t be able to receive payouts until your EIN arrives. You can see the ETA for EIN in your Atlas dashboard.

If you didn’t incorporate your company with Stripe Atlas, you’ll need to submit your EIN to before activating payments.

How Atlas calls the IRS on your behalf

When you use Atlas, you also sign IRS Form 8821. This form gives us permission to call the IRS to retrieve the EIN on your behalf. Using real-time data from the IRS, we call to retrieve the EIN as soon as we believe the IRS is processing applications from the time period we filed your request.

If your Stripe Atlas company was incorporated more than 10 business days ago, the IRS may have already issued your company’s EIN even if it’s not available in your Stripe dashboard yet.

Why it can take so long to get your EIN

The IRS requires us to fax your EIN filing to them, and they process these faxes manually. Sometimes when we call the IRS, they tell us that they can’t locate your company’s EIN filing and ask us to resubmit. This can happen multiple times, particularly in January and February when the IRS receives a large number of filings.

We’ll continue to call the IRS on your behalf, no matter how long it takes to retrieve your EIN. There are two optional steps you can take that may help us retrieve your EIN faster:

  • Call the IRS: Sometimes the IRS processes filings faster when the company founder calls them directly (instead of Atlas calling). See the next section below for instructions on calling the IRS. Hold times are typically 30 minutes.
  • Provide a US company address: The IRS often processes filings with a US company address faster than those with a non-US address. If you have a US address you can use to receive IRS correspondence (you can get a US address from our partner Stable), email support@stripe.com and we’ll update your EIN filing with this new address.

How to call the IRS to get your EIN

  • Make sure you are the Responsible Party on your company’s SS-4 form. Atlas lists the account opener as the Responsible Party.
  • The IRS will only share the EIN directly with your company’s Responsible Party, which you can find by looking at the signer of the SS-4 form.
  • You can view your SS-4 form in the Stripe Atlas Dashboard.
  • Have your SS-4 available ahead of your call.
  • The IRS agent will ask you questions about the company information on your SS-4 to confirm they’re authorized to give you the company’s EIN.
  • Call the IRS.
  • The best number to call is (+1) 800-829-4933. When you hear the various menu options, select option 1 for English or 2 for Spanish, then option 1 for EIN inquiries, and then option 3.
  • You can call during IRS Business hours: 7:00 a.m. - 7:00 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (GMT-5).
  • The shortest wait times are typically from 3:00 p.m. - 7:00 p.m ET. The longest wait times are typically between 8:00 am - 2:00 pm ET. Keep in mind, call wait times can be up to 1 hour long during busy periods.
  • Depending on your phone service and where you are located, there may be fees when calling the IRS. As wait times may be long (and can get costly!), you may want to check out services such as Google Voice or Skype.
  • What to say when speaking to an IRS representative:
  • “I’m calling to obtain the EIN for my company, [your company name here]. The SS-4 was faxed on [your company formation date], and I have not received my EIN number or letter.”
  • Atlas faxes the request to 855-641-6935, per the IRS’s instructions.
  • The IRS agent will ask some questions about your company. Have this information available when you call:
  • Be sure to use the exact information on the SS-4 form in your Stripe Atlas Dashboard.
  • Name of the company: Line 1 on SS-4
    • Spell out the letters in the company name
    • Be very clear on the company name
    • Inform the IRS if there are any spaces between the words or punctuation
    • The IRS system is extremely sensitive and will not locate your business if anything is incorrect
  • Responsible Party name: Line 7a on SS-4
  • Company address: Line 4a and 4b on SS-4
  • Date of formation: Line 11 on SS-4
  • Social Security Number (if you don’t have an SSN, say “Foreign”): Line 7b
  • Type of entity: Line 9a on SS-4
  • Title or position in the company: Inform the IRS you are the Responsible Party
  • The IRS will look up your company based on the information you’ve provided.
  • If the IRS has assigned the EIN, write down the number and request they fax the EIN to Legalinc (Stripe Atlas’s registered agent partner).
    • Use the fax number: 323-978-1998, and let the IRS know that someone is by the fax machine and ready to receive the fax.
    • If the IRS declines to fax it to Stripe Atlas, you can write the EIN number down and send it to atlas@stripe.com directly. We can then file it directly with your SS-4.
    • EINs may take up to 3 weeks to be assigned after your company has been formed. If it has been more than 3 weeks and you still have not received your EIN, Atlas may need to file a second copy of the request to make sure the IRS assigns your EIN.

How to pay Delaware franchise tax online

Delaware franchise tax is due on March 1st, 2026 and can be paid online through the state’s website. All Delaware C Corporations are required to pay this tax and file an Annual Report to maintain good standing. The tax amount varies, but for many companies, it’s likely to be a few hundred dollars instead of thousands.

Delaware franchise tax is due March 1st, 2026

  • Delaware offers two methods of calculating your franchise tax, and defaults to using one called the Authorized Shares method that often results in high tax bills.
  • Many Atlas companies can lower the amount of their tax bill significantly by calculating it online using the Assumed Par Value Capital method instead, by following this guide.
  • Atlas founders can also get discounted help on Delaware taxes, other state taxes you may owe, and Federal taxes from one of our tax partners or any tax advisor you choose.

What is Delaware franchise tax?

All Delaware C Corporations are required to pay the Delaware franchise Tax and to file an Annual Report. This is a tax charged by the state on all corporations registered in Delaware. It’s important to pay these taxes on time in order to keep your business in good standing and avoid penalties. Even companies with no revenue in the previous fiscal year should expect to pay some amount.

Perks towards tax advisors

Atlas partners with tax and accounting professionals who can help you file your state and federal taxes. View your options on the Atlas Perks page.

Stripe isn’t an accounting firm and can’t provide tax or accounting advice. Consult legal and tax professionals for advice on how to meet ongoing legal, tax, and accounting obligations that apply to you and your company.

How to pay Delaware franchise tax online

Stripe isn’t an accounting firm and can’t provide tax or accounting advice. Consult legal and tax professionals for advice on how to meet ongoing obligations that apply to your company. You can review the Stripe Atlas guide to business taxes before you get started.

Have the following handy before starting:

  • Your company documents from your Stripe Atlas Dashboard.
  • Form 1120 or recent balance sheet, if you haven’t yet filed taxes this year.
  • Physical company address from Stripe Atlas Dashboard.
  • Locate your seven digit Delaware Business Entity File Number. This is how you’ll log in to the Delaware website to pay your taxes.
Payment steps
  • Download your Filed Certificate of Incorporation in the Stripe Atlas Dashboard. View the second page of the Certificate of Incorporation to get your company’s Delaware Business Entity File Number.
  • Log in to the state of Delaware website using this Delaware Business Entity File Number.
  • Click the File Annual Report button. Be sure to click the correct tax year. Taxes for the 2025 tax year are paid in 2026.
  • Enter the number of issued shares.
    • The total number of shares will already be populated in the stock details section.
    • When you set up your company, you issue some of these shares to the founders. You can find how many shares you initially issued in your Founder Stock Board Consent in the Stripe Atlas Dashboard. If you have issued any additional shares this year, be sure to include those in the number of issued shares.
  • Enter your Gross Assets.
    • Gross assets, or total assets, can be found on your federal corporate income tax (IRS Form 1120, Schedule L). If you haven’t yet filed this year’s corporate income tax, you can use a recent balance sheet for this number.
  • Enter your Asset Date. This will be the last day of this year in which you are filing these taxes (12/31/202X).
  • Enter your End Date of Fiscal Year. This will be 12/31 of this year, unless you’ve filed to change your fiscal year with the IRS. In that case, use the last day of your fiscal year.
  • Click Recalculate Tax button to see how much tax you owe for the year.
    • This button can take some time to load.
    • Most companies formed with Stripe Atlas will see the amount they owe decrease. By default, and in any tax notices, Delaware calculates tax owed using the Authorized Shares method. Most Atlas companies find they pay less tax when they use the Assumed Par Value Capital method instead of the default Authorized Shares method.
    • View the new Amount due above the table. The minimum tax amount due is $400 (plus $50 Annual Filing Fee).
  • Enter your Employer Identification Number from the IRS. View your company page to view your EIN in the Stripe Atlas Dashboard.
  • Enter your company address. Enter the company’s physical location. If you don’t yet have a company office, you can use your home address.
  • Enter your one company officer’s name and details. You only need to enter one company officer’s information. This can be either your President or Secretary. You can check your officer roles in your Filed Certificate of Incorporation in the Stripe Atlas Dashboard.
  • Enter company director information
    • Enter your current number of Directors in the number box. After you enter the number, you can click Enter Directors Info.
    • The form will generate a row for each director. For example, entering “2” creates two rows to enter information.
    • You can check your initial Directors in your Board Approval in the Stripe Atlas Dashboard. If your Board has changed, be sure to enter the most up to date list of directors.
  • Authorize your company’s information. Fill out all the required information to attest to the accuracy of the information.
  • After you verify you entered all of the correct information, click the green Proceed to Payment button. You can choose to pay Delaware Franchise Tax and Annual Report filing fee either by credit card or ACH. After inputting your payment information, click the green Submit button to finish.

You can save your work and return to it later, just make sure to save your session number, which the Delaware portal gives you the option of sending to an email address for easier access.

If you have additional questions regarding Delaware state taxes, you can work with one of our tax partners.

Key tax dates for Atlas companies

All Atlas companies are incorporated in Delaware and are considered domestic United States companies. Atlas companies will owe Delaware franchise taxes (for C-corps) or annual fees (for LLCs) and must file federal taxes for each year after forming, unless they choose to dissolve the company. Companies may have annual tax and compliance obligations in other states they do business.

Below are the Delaware and federal tax due dates that apply to all Atlas companies.

Many companies have additional state and federal filing obligations in addition to those listed below. Atlas partners can help companies understand in which states outside Delaware they have tax and compliance obligations. Our tax and accounting partners can help companies file their taxes and track additional requirements specific to the company’s operations.

Key filing dates for all Atlas companies

It’s a good idea to mark your calendars for the following filing dates! Atlas will email you with reminders and additional resources in advance of key deadlines for Delaware filings and federal tax filings.

  • February 2, 2026: Deadline for employers to distribute W-2 forms to employees and 1099 forms to independent contractors for the previous tax year.
  • March 1, 2026: Delaware Franchise Tax filing due for Atlas C-corps (including subsidiaries).
  • April 15, 2026: Deadline for federal income tax filing (or to file form 7004 for a 6 month extension).
  • June 1, 2026: Delaware Annual Fee filing due for Atlas LLCs.
  • October 15, 2026: Deadline for federal income tax if you filed an extension in April.
  • December 31, 2026: Deadline for making any year end tax deductions and contributions.

Common filing dates for companies operating in New York and California

Many startups may also need to register for business in New York or California (our partners can help you determine if you need to register). For companies registered in these states, see additional key dates below.

  • March 2, 2026: San Francisco Business Tax filing due (any companies that conduct business in San Francisco).
  • April 15, 2026: New York state franchise tax for C-corps.
  • April 15, 2026: California state franchise tax for C-corps.

Legal and tax help for your Stripe Atlas company

Tax and accounting help

As US companies, all Atlas companies need to file state and federal taxes each year. Federal business taxes are due by April 15, 2025, or October 15, 2025 if you file an extension.

Taxes you may need to pay

Businesses incorporated in Delaware usually need to pay:

  • US federal and state corporate income tax. The federal government and most US states tax the income of your company. We recommend you work with a tax professional to help you file. Federal income tax is due by April 15, 2025 (or by October 15, 2025, if you file an extension). State income tax due dates may vary; check your state government website for details.
  • Delaware tax. An annual tax due March 1 for Delaware C corporations and June 1 for Delaware LLCs, which is generally a few hundred dollars for startups. Learn how to file or get help from our partners.
  • Sales tax. Many states and cities—and some countries—charge tax on the sale of products and services. A tax professional can help you file your sales tax reports as well, while Stripe Tax can automate the calculation and collection of sales tax on your transactions.

Even if you had no revenue, you likely still need to file taxes for 2023. If your business is no longer operational, consider dissolving your company to avoid paying taxes in future tax years.

How to get help

Atlas partners with tax and accounting professionals who can help you file your state and federal taxes. Check out our full set of partners in the Perks page of your Atlas Dashboard.

  • Pilot is great for startups that raised or are planning to raise funding, who want recurring tax and bookkeeping services for state and federal taxes.
  • Fondo is also great for startups seeking full service tax and accounting help. Atlas C Corporations get 50% off all plans their first year.
  • Legalinc provides end-to-end Delaware franchise tax filing, including annual report preparation, filing, and tax payment submission with no extra steps or state-site checkout. Atlas founders get 10% off.
  • If you have an accounting and tax team in house, software from Puzzle, Quickbooks, and Xero can help them manage your books more easily.

Legal advice

Stripe Atlas is unable to provide legal or accounting advice.

If you require legal advice, but don’t have your own counsel, Soxton is an online legal services firm offering free, 15 minute consultations and fixed fee packages for common Stripe Atlas company needs.

If you plan to raise venture capital and want ongoing legal services from a top tier startup law firm, Atlas can facilitate an introduction to our partners at Cooley LLP. Please request an introduction by emailing atlas-cooley@stripe.com. Companies with a US company address only.

Note: Stripe isn’t an accounting firm and can’t provide tax or accounting advice. Consult legal and tax professionals for advice on how to meet ongoing legal, tax, and accounting obligations that apply to you and your company.

Managing your registered agent subscription

Companies formed in Delaware must maintain a “registered agent” to act as your liaison with the state and to receive legal notices if the company is sued. Your first year of registered agent services is included in your one-time Stripe Atlas fee.

Renewing your registered agent subscription

To make maintaining this service easy for you, Stripe Atlas automatically renews registered agent services each year by charging your credit card for that year’s renewal fee annually on your company formation date. The renewal fee is $100, and it will be charged to your credit card on file each year. You can update your payment method in the Stripe Dashboard.

If your address or contact information has changed, please update your details in the Atlas section of the Stripe Dashboard so that we can process your registered agent renewal on time.

Cancelling your registered agent subscription

If you’d like to opt out of the renewal of your registered agent services, you can cancel your subscription in the Stripe Dashboard. If you choose to opt out of this subscription and are not dissolving your company, you will need to make your own arrangements to appoint a Delaware registered agent in order for your company to remain in good standing with the state of Delaware.

Payments and banking before receiving your EIN

Atlas automatically gets your company an IRS tax ID, called an Employer Identification Number (EIN), after filing your incorporation in Delaware. You can start accepting US card payments on Stripe, open a Stripe Treasury financial account, transfer your Stripe balance to an external bank account, and begin fundraising before the IRS assigns your EIN.

Other third party services may require your EIN before you can start using their products. The IRS typically processes EIN applications in 1-2 business days if you provide a US company address, a US company phone number, and a US social security number. If you don’t submit any of those three datapoints, the IRS could take 6-8 weeks. Atlas will email you when your EIN is available.

Accepting payments before receiving your EIN

You can activate US card payments on Stripe for your Atlas company before receiving your EIN. Stripe offers no-code payment options, including Payment Links and Invoices, and all Atlas companies get $2,500 in Stripe product credits for your first year after incorporation

Atlas will email you once your company is incorporated in Delaware (typically 1-2 business days after you submit your application). You can activate Stripe Payments from that email, or from your Atlas Dashboard, and Atlas will automatically pre-fill fields that you already filled out during your Atlas application. You’ll need to submit a US phone number (our partners in the Perks section of the Atlas Dashboard can help if you need one).

You can transfer your Stripe balance to a bank account before your EIN arrives, up to $100,000 USD, following the first payout waiting period. You can access additional payment methods beyond US card payments only once your EIN is available.

Note: this experience is currently available for companies incorporated on or after September 3, 2025. If you incorporated before this date, have not yet received your EIN, and want to activate payments or payouts, please contact support and we’ll help you get started.

Opening a financial account before receiving your EIN

Stripe Treasury allows Atlas companies to open financial accounts before you receive your EIN. Launch an application from the Atlas Perks page to get started. You can begin transferring your Stripe balance to your financial account after you receive your EIN.

Additional Atlas banking partners, and most other banking providers, require you to submit your EIN before you start banking.

What else you can do before receiving your EIN

You can begin fundraising before receiving your EIN with AngelList, which supports new cap table accounts without an EIN. Many engineering, organization, and product tools don’t require an EIN to get started.

You can confirm the onboarding requirements for additional Atlas partners by clicking on them in the Perks section of the Atlas Dashboard.

What you cannot do before receiving your EIN

It’s likely that you’ll need to wait for your EIN before hiring new employees and registering for business in states outside Delaware, but you may be able to start setting up your account with payroll and compliance tools while you wait.

You can confirm the onboarding requirements for additional Atlas partners by clicking on them in the Perks section of the Atlas Dashboard.

Reporting company ownership to FinCEN

Companies formed on Atlas are not required to report Beneficial Ownership Information (BOI) to the US Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), per new guidance issued on March 21 2025.

Do any Atlas companies have to report to FinCEN?

No. All Atlas companies are domestic U.S. companies and are not required to report information on their beneficial owners to FinCEN under the most recent guidance. This is true for all company types (new C-corp, subsidiary, and LLC) formed on Atlas and true for Atlas companies that have non-US founders.

Non-US parent companies of an Atlas subsidiary may be required to report.

Read more at FinCEN’s website.

What if I already reported?

No further action is required. You do not need to report changes to your original report, nor take any action to retract it or follow up.

What if I the guidance changes?

We’ll update this support article and communicate with users if the guidance changes such that any Atlas company is required to report beneficial ownership information to FinCEN.

Where can I learn more?

  • FinCEN’s website and reference materials
  • FinCEN explainer from our partners at Cooley LLP

More resources will be added as they become available.

[Last updated March 26, 2025.]

Note: Stripe isn’t a law firm or an accounting firm and can’t provide legal, tax or accounting advice. Consult legal and tax professionals for advice on how to meet ongoing legal, tax, and accounting obligations for you and your company.

Stripe Atlas restricted business categories

Atlas does not permit businesses that sell illegal products or services, promote violence, or otherwise violate our Terms of Service. By submitting an Atlas application, you agree not to operate in any of the following unsupported business categories.

Business categories restricted from Atlas

Atlas does not support businesses in or related to the following categories:

  • Illegal drugs: Production, promotion, or sales of illegal drugs. This includes sales and auxiliary businesses related to marijuana, and products that mimic illegal drugs.
  • Marketing certain products to minors: Businesses that market alcohol, tobacco, or sexual products directly or exclusively to children under 18 years old. This may include flavored tobacco products, electronic or otherwise.
  • Unauthorized or unregulated financial services: Shell banks, anonymous financial accounts, and predatory lending services.
  • Hazardous or restricted materials: Toxic, explosive, flammable, or radioactive materials and EPA-restricted pesticides.
  • Offensive or discriminatory products: Content, products or services that promote hate or violence, or discriminate against legally protected classes.
  • Unregulated health services: Unregistered medical benefit packages, pseudo-pharmaceuticals with unsubstantiated claims, or unapproved therapeutic drugs.
  • Intellectual property infringements: Counterfeit or unauthorized use of IP, and unauthorized resale of goods.
  • Weapons and violence: Firearms, ammunition, weapons components, or other products that enable violence.
  • Deceptive or unethical practices: Get-rich-quick schemes, document falsification, unauthorized payment facilitation, telecommunication manipulation, and expired or harmful products.

Business categories Atlas supports, but which may not be supported on Stripe Payments

Please note that other Stripe products (including payments) may have additional eligibility requirements.Atlas can form businesses in or related to the following categories, but these categories may be restricted from using Stripe Payments due to their presence on Stripe’s general list of prohibited businesses.

  • Adult content and services: Pornography, dating websites, and sexually oriented products.
  • Debt and credit services: Debt collections, credit repair/monitoring, and debt relief companies.
  • Cryptocurrency: Trading, wallets, mining, ICOs, and yield accounts.
  • Gambling and betting: Online or brick-and-mortar casinos, lotteries, and skill games with prizes.
  • Non-fungible tokens (NFTs): First or secondary sales, marketplace platforms, and SaaS solutions related to NFT’s.
  • Identity services and insurance: Identify monitoring, recovery, and identity theft insurance.
  • Certain financial legal services: Bankruptcy lawyers, bail bonds, and payday lenders.
  • Digital promotion products: Selling traffic or followers to websites or social media accounts.
  • Travel organizations: Airlines, timeshares, and cruises that pose heightened financial risk.

Waived payments processing fees for Atlas users

Atlas companies incorporated before October 16, 2025 get waived fees on Stripe payments for 1 year after incorporation, on your first $100,000 USD in revenue. Companies incorporated on or after October 16, 2025 get a new, more flexible offer ($2,500 credits on Stripe products).

Which Atlas users are eligible for Stripe processing credits?

All Atlas companies are eligible for these credits after incorporating. You cannot transfer your credits from your Atlas Stripe account to another Stripe Account.

How do I activate these credits?

The credits will activate automatically for all Atlas companies, on the day your Atlas company is incorporated. The 1 year term starts on this day.

No further action is required to activate your credits, and you’ll see them applied upon paying out your Stripe balance (as a deduction of fees). Read more about how waived fees work.

Can these credits be stacked with other Stripe offers?

Yes. Atlas users with other Stripe payments processing offers can stack their credits. Stripe will automatically use the credit offer with the earlier expiration date first.

You can view your different credits offers in the Balances tab of your Stripe Dashboard. Read more.

Can you extend the timeline / size of the Atlas processing credits?

Unfortunately, we cannot extend the eligibility window beyond 1 year or beyond your first $100,000 in revenue.

What taxes (Delaware and federal) do I owe as a U.S. company?

Your company should expect to pay taxes each year it is in existence. For a general information on what types of tax returns U.S. businesses must file, you can check out the Stripe Atlas guide on business taxes. This guide will help you understand some of the considerations to estimate the taxes for your company:

  • Taxpayer ID numbers
  • Delaware Franchise Tax
  • Sales Tax
  • Corporate income tax
  • LLC federal income tax
  • Transfer pricing

For more details on tax obligations including key tax season dates, filing taxes, tax partners and more, you can check out the Stripe Atlas docs on taxes.

For information on automatically collecting sales tax on Stripe transactions, check out Stripe Tax.

Which address should I use for Atlas incorporation?

Different steps of your company setup have different address requirements.

If you have a U.S. physical address

You can use it everywhere — it works for every step of incorporation, Stripe payments, and banking.

If you don’t have a U.S. physical address

You may need a virtual U.S. address for some steps. You can get one through our Atlas partner Stable.

Each step has different requirements:

  • Incorporation: Any address works, U.S. or non-U.S., except your registered agent address.
  • Stripe payments: You can use a physical or virtual U.S. address.
  • Banking: Most banks require a physical address. Stripe Treasury and some banking partners accept non-U.S. physical addresses.

Can I use my registered agent address?

No. Atlas appoints your registered agent to receive mail from the Delaware Secretary of State. Don’t use this address for incorporation or banking.

Why did Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 decline my Stripe-issued Treasury card?

Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 might decline your Stripe-issued Treasury card if the billing address registered with them doesn’t match your card’s billing address. The error message might be generic, such as “Address doesn’t match.”

Resolve a billing address mismatch

  • Find your card’s billing address in the Stripe Dashboard.
  • Compare it with the billing address registered with Google Workspace or Microsoft 365.
  • Make sure the addresses match by either:
    • Updating your card’s billing address to match your Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 address.
    • Updating your Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 address to match your card’s billing address.
  • Retry the purchase.

How Stripe determines your card’s billing address

When you incorporate through Stripe Atlas and onboard to Stripe Treasury and Cards, Stripe creates a cardholder using the account representative’s address. This address can be inside or outside the United States and becomes the billing address for cards issued to that cardholder.

You can create additional cardholders after incorporation, but they must have a US address.

Billing

2020 Visa Trial Subscription Requirement Changes FAQ

Visa is changing their rules governing free-trial and promotion driven subscriptions on April 18, 2020. Stripe is actively working to make sure that your business has the information it needs to be compliant with the new rules. We have included the following FAQs to help you understand the changes and you can read more about it on Visa’s Trial Subscription Updates flier. If you have additional questions, contact Stripe Support.

DO THESE CHANGES APPLY TO ME?

  • I offer a subscription that does not have a free or promotional trial. Do these changes apply to me? No, these rule changes do not apply to you.
  • I always offer coupons to new customers, does that count as promotional? No, if you offer every new customer a discount regardless of the type subscription, these changes do not apply to you. Only free and promotional trial subscription merchants (such as seasonal offerings, etc.) need to comply.
  • I don’t collect credit card information when I set up a free trial. Do these changes apply to me? No, these changes don’t apply to you because a customer is actively giving you card information for a paid subscription vs. setting up a free trial that automatically converts to a paid subscription.

WHAT CHANGES ARE BEING PROPOSED AND WHY?

  • Why are subscription rules changing? Subscriptions can sometimes cause customer confusion, especially when free and promotional subscriptions charge customers long after signing up. The subscription rules are changing in the interest of protecting consumers and making it clear to them when and how much they will be charged.
  • What is “negative response” and “negative option” marketing?“Negative response” and “negative option” marketing is where the default option is that the customer is charged for a product or service, without any action on their behalf. It can create a poor customer experience, if the customer thinks they have been charged without an opportunity to decline or cancel. These new rules are, in part, a response to an increase in this type of marketing.
  • How can Stripe help me comply? Stripe builds compliant products by design. For users who have built a unique subscription customer experience, we will help identify the areas that you need to update.

WHAT CHANGES DO I NEED TO MAKE?

  • My customer now has to opt-in to a subscription, how do I do this? The main goal is to make sure customers are clear about the terms of a subscription. The network rules require that you obtain express consent prior to collecting payment information (referred to as “customer opt-in”) to the following core aspects of the trial trial or promotion:
    • Subscription Terms
    • Frequency of charges and amount
    • Terms of Cancellation
    • Cancellation Policy

We will not dictate how you obtain this consent, that will depend on the nature of your business. However, depending on your Stripe integration, we do provide functionality that can help facilitate your compliance (for example, if you use Stripe Checkout, compliant card mandated language will be displayed).

  • I do not offer electronic cancellation of subscriptions, is that acceptable? Unfortunately no, you need to build an online or SMS way for your customers to cancel their subscription. If you are a Stripe Billing user, see “I’m a Stripe Billing user, do these changes apply to me?” below. You can also use the customer portal to provide customers the ability to cancel their subscription.
  • Does the timing of the trial expiration email and the initial confirmation matter? The most important thing is to give your customers clear information about the terms and conditions of subscription they just signed up for. The networks give you the option to include information about the trial expiration in the initial email but your business should decide if you want to send your customer this information separately.
  • What if a free trial is less than 7 days? That’s acceptable; you don’t have to change the trial period. You just have to let your customers know when the free trial ends and the terms and conditions of your cancellation policy.
  • Do I have to email my customer 7 days before every new subscription charge? No, you only need to send the reminder before the date that it converts to a paid subscription. The subsequent transactions can be processed according to the terms and conditions that you and the customer agreed to before completing the purchase.
  • What is an Enhanced Merchant Descriptor? The goal of this rule is to ensure that when a free or promotional subscription transitions into a paid subscription, a customer can quickly identify it in their credit card statement. This means that the first amount charged should use the enhanced descriptor. The networks do not specify what it should say, but it should display something that makes it stand out (e.g.,* TRIAL END*).
  • How does this change how I respond to Subscription-related disputes? Any disputes related to subscription charges after April 18, 2020 need to adhere to the new rules. As a result, if you do not make the required changes and a customer disputes the charge, you will lose by default. To ensure that your business can continue to dispute invalid chargebacks, make the changes by April 18, 2020.
  • I am a Stripe Billing user, do these changes apply to me? As with any network changes, it is the responsibility of each business to determine what is within scope for you. Stripe Billing does have solutions to help make complying with rule changes easier if you choose to use it.
    • We have existing tools like email reminders and receipts that will be updated with new requirements.
    • Stripe Billing provides the customer portal, a hosted solution where customers will be able to manage their subscriptions and billing details.
    • If you do not host trial information with Stripe Billing or use other tools in conjunction with Stripe Billing, we recommend reviewing your customer/product flows to understand what adjustments you might need to make.

Add a one-time fee or discount with a new subscription plan

To include a one-time charge or discount to the first subscription invoice, you can do so by adding an invoice item to the customer before creating the subscription. This can be done using the API or directly in the Stripe Dashboard.

Add an invoice item using the API

Example code for adding an invoice item using the API can be found in our Subscription Invoices documentation.

Add an invoice item through the Dashboard

To add an invoice item in the Dashboard:

  • Find and click on the customer in your Customers list.
  • Under Pending Invoice Items, click + Add invoice item.
  • Add the description, amount, and currency, and select Auto (next to be billed) from the Subscription dropdown.
  • Click Create invoice item.

From there, add the subscription to the customer, and the invoice will generate for the cost of the subscription and the additional pending invoice item.
