Refunds in Mexico

Most common questions and guidance on how to manage refunds in your Mexico Stripe account.

  • Creating a refund – how to refund a payment using Stripe API or Dashboard?

You can refund non-disputed payments to your customers using the Stripe API or directly from the Dashboard.

From the Dashboard

  • Find the charge to be refunded in the Payments overview page.
  • Click the ••• icon to the right of the charge and select Refund charge.
  • Enter the amount to be refunded. The default is a full refund. For a partial refund, enter a different amount to be refunded.
  • Select a reason for the refund. If you select Other, you must provide an explanatory note that is attached to the refund.
  • Click Refund.

Using the Stripe API

  • Create a create_refund call in the API.

  • In the API call, include the charge ID to refund.

  • To refund an amount different than the full charge amount, include the amount parameter and enter the amount to refund. If no amount is entered, the default action will be a refund of the full charge amount.

  • Run the API call.

  • Canceling a refund – how can I cancel a refund?

For a short window of time after creation, some card refunds support cancellations via the dashboard. The refund must not have been processed as a charge reversal. If cancellation is no longer available, you would need to create a new charge for the customer in the amount of the refund in order to recoup the funds.

  • Refunding to prevent disputes – can I refund a payment to prevent a dispute?

Yes – if you suspect a charge could be fraudulent, it is recommended to refund it instead of letting it be disputed. If selling physical products, refund cardholders who do not wish to wait for items that are expected to be delayed longer than the originally communicated shipping time. The refund should be issued to their original payment method rather than providing store credit. To avoid disputes & refunds, ensure that product descriptions, product images, item conditions, return policy, refund policy, and any money-back guarantees are accurate, clearly listed, and easily understood.

  • Refund timeline – how long does it take for a refund to be processed in Mexico?

From a merchant perspective, refunds are processed in Mexico in up to two business days on your Stripe account. The cardholder’s refund takes place up until 15 days after the refund has been processed but this process varies from issuer to issuer, which means may be received earlier or later than expected.

  • Missing refund – what should I do if my customer doesn’t receive a refund in the expected timeline?

The cardholder should get in touch with the issuer if the refund does not take place in 15 days.

  • Closed account – what happens to a refund if the bank account is closed?

In general, issuers will allow the refund to be processed and accept the funds. If the cardholder has the same card issuer and bank account, then funds will be successfully credited to that account. If the cardholder has not yet seen the refund after 15 days on their account and it looks successful on Stripe’s side, they should contact their financial institution.

  • Refund fees – are Stripe fees also refunded when processing a refund?

There are no fees to refund a payment, but Stripe’s fees on the original payment will not be returned in case of a refund. A large portion of the underlying cost of payment processing is driven by fees assessed by banks and payment networks (like Visa and Mastercard). These networks set rules about which fees apply for refunded payments, and in many cases banks and card networks keep the entire upfront cost of a refunded transaction. For some regions and payment types, refunded payments also incur additional fees.

We aim to make our pricing simple and transparent, and our standard fees include access to a variety of features like fraud protection, reporting, and other tools for managing your payments. To address these underlying payment processing costs and continue providing these services as part of our standard pricing, Stripe does not return our fees when a payment is refunded.

  • Insufficient funds for refund – how can I top up my account to cover a refund?

You can add funds to cover existing negative balances or proactively add funds to be used for future refunds or chargebacks that will be held separately from your earnings, payouts, and funds from other Stripe products. To do so, go to the section ‘Saldos’ in your Dashboard and click on the option ‘Agregar al Saldo’.

The funds added through this process are used to cover for refunds and chargebacks only. If you are using Connect and looking to add funds to pay out to connected accounts, this option is still not available in Mexico.

  • Closed account – How do refunds and disputes are managed after closing a Stripe account?

Even if the account has been closed, the account owner will still be responsible for any refunds that are issued or any disputes that arise. Due to this, it is normally suggested to leave the account dormant rather than closing it altogether, as this makes it easier to be responsive if these situations occur.

Understanding refund statuses

Refunds move through multiple statuses before successfully reconciling to the customer’s balance. You might need to take action for certain types of statuses.

Refunded

The refund has been successfully initiated from Stripe. This doesn’t guarantee that the refund has landed on the customer’s side. After the required processing time of 5-10 business days, your customer should receive their refund.

In the Dashboard Payments tab, click the transaction to view more details about it. If available, find the reference number by clicking View Details under the Timeline.

Reversed

The refund has been initiated as a reversal. The original payment will not show up on your customer’s bank statement. The status is usually accompanied by a System Trace Audit Number (STAN) on the Dashboard payment page for the transaction.

Partial refund and Partially reversed

These are similar to Refunded and Reversed, except the refund that’s been initiated is for part of the original transaction amount. To see the refunded amount, go to the Dashboard Payments tab and hover over the info icon of the transaction.

Refund pending

The refund hasn’t been initiated for one of the following three reasons. Hover over the Refund Pending status in the Dashboard Payments tab to determine the reason the refund is pending.

Financial partner or bank processing

Some refunds are pending while our financial partner or customer’s bank is processing them. You don’t need to take any further action.

Payment is not settled

Some refunds are pending because the refunding payment is still processing and has not been settled. You don’t need to take any further action.

Insufficient funds

The refund is pending due to an insufficient balance in your Stripe account. To unblock the refund process, follow the steps in Fix your pending refund.

Reporting

Common Reporting Standard (CRS) self-certification

Complete your CRS tax self-certification

If Stripe asks you to complete a Common Reporting Standard (CRS) self-certification, complete the form through the Account status page in your Stripe Dashboard.

Why Stripe asks for this information

CRS is an international standard for sharing financial account information between tax authorities to help prevent tax evasion. Stripe collects your tax residency and account holder classification to meet tax reporting requirements.

This is separate from identity verification. Your country of tax residence can differ from where your business operates, and you can have more than one tax residence.

Complete the form
  • Sign in to the Stripe Dashboard and open Account status.
  • Open the task requesting CRS tax self-certification.
  • Review your details and confirm or correct the suggested classification. Enter each country of tax residence and its tax identification number (TIN).
  • Complete any additional questions, review your answers, and sign and submit the form before the deadline shown in the task.
Understand your account holder classification

The form distinguishes individuals from legal entities and asks legal entities to confirm their classification:

  • Individual: A person holding the account in their own name, including a sole proprietor.
  • Active non-financial entity (Active NFE): A non-financial business that meets the CRS active-entity criteria. Operating businesses, such as retailers, manufacturers, and software companies, commonly fall into this category.
  • Passive non-financial entity (Passive NFE): A non-financial entity that doesn’t qualify as an Active NFE, often because it primarily earns passive income, such as interest or dividends.
  • Financial institution: An entity that takes deposits, holds financial assets for others, conducts qualifying investment activities, or provides certain insurance products.
  • Investment entity managed by another financial institution: An entity whose income primarily comes from investing, reinvesting, or trading financial assets and whose assets are managed by another financial institution.

If prompted, provide information about controlling persons—the individuals who ultimately own or control the entity.

These descriptions are a summary. See the OECD’s entity self-certification guidance or consult your tax adviser if you’re unsure which classification applies.

Customizing Your Reports

Report Filters

You can filter your reports further by date, amount, payment success status, or payment method by clicking ‘Filter’ on the upper left corner of the page.

Adding Custom Columns

When exporting reports, you can also have the option of having multiple metadata fields included in your reports, including card brand, product description, and country of customer, among other fields. To do this,

  • On the top right corner of the Payment page, click Export

  • In the resulting view’s Column section, click Custom and ensure that the desired metadata columns are checked

If you have any custom metadata columns added to your payments, these columns will be included in the exports by default. Though metadata is not explicitly listed on the available columns, exporting the report will automatically include the metadata.

If you have examined the available columns (make sure to select ‘All’ columns to review all the available data) and can’t find what you’re looking for there are two options.

First option: If the data does not currently exist in Stripe, you could consider adding this information as Metadata to customers, payments or other data within Stripe. You can then export this metadata alongside the customers, charges, or other data it relates to.

Second option: If the information already exists within Stripe, or you’re simply looking for more advanced options for analyzing all available information, you can consider using Stripe Sigma to write custom SQL queries across your data.

Exporting a report of all transactions

We recommend using the Balance Summary Report for your accounting and reconciliation needs.

This report functions similarly to a bank statement, providing an CSV and PDF export of your complete transaction history that impacts your Stripe balance — including successfully processed payments, refunds, disputes, and fees — making it ideal for reconciling your Stripe account balance at the end of each month.

For more information on other reports recommended for financial reconciliation, see how to select a report.

Other ways to manage your transactions

To track and analyze your payment performance, check out Payments Analytics.

For searching and managing individual payments, head to Exporting Payment data.

Exporting Fees Paid

There are two reports in the Stripe Dashboard that show your fees, depending on how much detail you need.

Fees Report

The Fees Report is the best place to see a dedicated breakdown of what you’ve been charged in Stripe fees. It shows fees at the transaction and product level, so you can see exactly what contributed to your total fees for a given period.

To export your fees from the Fees Report:

  • Navigate to Reporting > Fees in the Dashboard.
  • Apply your preferred date range and any other filters.

Balance Summary Report

If you want to see your fees alongside the rest of your funds movement — such as payments, refunds, and payouts — use the Balance Summary Report instead. This gives you a full picture of how your balance changed over a given period, with fees shown as one component.

To view fees in the Balance Summary Report:

  • Navigate to Reporting > Balance Summary in the Dashboard.
  • Apply your preferred date range, timezone, and any other filters.

Invoices for Stripe fees

In certain countries, Stripe will generate an invoice for the fees you’ve incurred each month which you can use for tax purposes. Refer to our guide on downloading your tax invoices for more information.

Retrieving fees programmatically

Both the Fees Report and the Balance Summary Report can be run through the Stripe Reports API. This is useful if you want to automate report generation or integrate fee data into your own systems.

If you’d like to retrieve the fees for a given payment programmatically, follow the guide in our docs.

Exporting Reports as PDF

Export your Balance Summary Reports and Payout Reconciliation Report as PDF files directly from the Stripe Dashboard. The exported PDF includes Stripe letterhead, your account ID, legal entity information, and the figures for your selected date range.

How to export a report as PDF

  • In the Dashboard, navigate to Reporting > Balance Summary Reports or Payout Reconciliation Report
  • Apply the relevant filters, such as the date range and timezone.
  • On the section of the report you’d like to export, click Export.
  • In the pop-up, select PDF as the file format.
  • Choose your preferred report format and currencies, then click Download PDF.

Report formats

There are two report formats available:

  • Summary — Shows the total figures for the selected period.
  • Itemized — Shows a row-by-row breakdown of every transaction that contributed to the summary totals.

The PDF itemized report format is limited to 5,000 rows.

Other report types

Most other Stripe reports are available for export as CSV only. To export a CSV report, navigate to the relevant report page in the Dashboard and click Export.

Fees report FAQ

The Fees report shows fees taken from your Stripe balance, credits balance, and financial accounts. Fees from Stripe, networks, and external partners for your use of Stripe products and services are included.

  • How often does the fee report update?
  • How much of my account’s past fee data can I access?
  • Does the report cover all fees?
  • Can I report on fees across currencies?
  • How do I use the date filter?
  • How can I view descriptions of fees in the fees report?
  • Why do I see negative fee items?
  • Why am I seeing a row with only the tax amount?
  • What are round offs and how do I attribute them?
  • Can there be multiple fees on a single payment?
  • Why are some fees attributed to Payment Intent IDs instead of Charge IDs?
  • Can I view fees by transaction?
  • Can I exclude the PayPal passthrough fee from the report?
  • Do Stripe fees change after they’re created? How long after they’re created can they change?
  • How can I use this itemized dataset?
  • How can I reconcile this report with other Stripe reports?
  • How is the itemized_fees dataset on Stripe Sigma and Data Pipeline different from itemized fees exported on the Dashboard?

How often does the fee report update?

The report shows fee data 96 hours after a fee has settled from one of your balances.

How much of my account’s past fee data can I access?

You can review data from as early as January 2022, however data prior to January 2024 may be incomplete. We recommend searching for data from January 2024 onwards.

Does the report cover all fees?

The report includes fees that impact the account’s Stripe balance, credits balance, and financial accounts, with some exceptions:

  • Included in the report: PayPal passthrough fees deducted from the PayPal account.
    • If you settle PayPal payments to PayPal, the passthrough fee is deducted from your PayPal account.
  • Excluded from the report: Terminal device purchases, Stripe Capital fees, Atlas fees, and post-paid invoiced fees.

Can I report on fees across currencies?

Yes, the Fees report shows fees in multiple currencies. Fees are reported in their settlement currency. You can switch between currencies using the currency filter.

How do I use the date filter?

“Incurred at” filter

Use the “incurred at” filter to show fee data based on the date of the originating activity that incurred the fee.

Example: To show a fee assessed on February 1st for a charge created on January 31st, run the report for January.

“Balance transaction date” filter

Use the “balance transaction date” filter to show fee data based on the date of the fee assessment, not the originating activity.

Example: To show a fee assessed on February 1st for a charge created on January 31st, filter by balance transaction date and run the report for February.

How can I view descriptions of fees in the fees report?

To view a description for each fee, turn on Show descriptions in the report.

Why do I see negative fee items?

Fee line items with a negative value are amounts that are “credited” to the user’s balance. This can happen when the user gets a fee refunded.

Why am I seeing a row with only the tax amount?

Stripe users based in certain countries and areas may have taxes on Stripe fees. If the total taxed amount for a Stripe fee is less than 1 cent, the amount less than 1 cent is subtracted.

Example: If the total taxed amount is 0.0135, Stripe subtracts 0.0035 to round it down to 1 cent.

What are round offs and how do I attribute them?

Stripe rounds the Stripe fee to the nearest unit, such as pence. Example: If the fee is 0.025, Stripe rounds up to 0.03. If the fee is 0.024, Stripe rounds down to 0.02.

For gross settled or async fees, round offs are applied to the invoice amount rather than a single transaction. Therefore, a round off can’t be attributed to a single transaction, and in these cases incurred_by is set to balance_transaction_id which is linked to the invoice.

Can there be multiple fees on a single payment?

When your account creates multiple failed charges for a single payment, Stripe attributes verification fees (such as 3DS or per-auth fees) for all the failed charges to the related payment.

Why are some fees attributed to Payment Intent IDs instead of Charge IDs?

This happens when fees (such as 3DS or per-authorization fees) are associated with failed charges.

Because failed charge IDs are not exposed in the Stripe API, the report surfaces the Payment Intent ID (pi_) so you can still query and reconcile these fees. To understand the full cost of a transaction, you may need to aggregate fees across both the Payment Intent ID and any successful Charge IDs (ch_) associated with it.

Can I view fees by transaction?

Yes, download the report and select the option to export an itemized view of the fee dataset. This view displays granular fee reporting, broken out by fee type and linked back to the transaction that incurred the fee.

Can I exclude the PayPal passthrough fee from the report?

No, the PayPal fee you see covers two charges: Stripe’s processing fee (deducted from your Stripe account balance) and PayPal’s passthrough fees (charged to your PayPal account or Stripe balance, depending on your PayPal funds settings).

For a detailed breakdown of PayPal passthrough fees, log in to PayPal and review your PayPal Settlement Report.

Do Stripe fees change after they’re created? How long after they’re created can they change?

If you’re on the IC+ pricing model, month-end fees are subject to revisions. We may adjust network costs for up to two months after the transaction occurs. Example: You can expect to see revisions for May transactions until the July 1st billing, with final amounts available by July 3rd.

Adjustments may occur to previously deducted fees as Stripe receives additional data from financial partners regarding transactions. These monthly fee adjustments ensure that we’re charging accurate billing, so fees for a given period may be updated in the following months.

Learn more about the Interchange Plus (IC+) pricing model.

How can I use this itemized dataset?

  • To see the fees associated with a particular charge ID or payout, filter or group by the incurred_by column. It will show an itemized list of fees incurred by a given transaction.
  • To see the breakdown of fees relating to a particular settlement transaction or money movement, filter or group by balance_transaction_id or fee_transaction_id.
    • If a fee credit or financial account was used to cover all or part of the fee amount, you’ll see a fee_transaction_id. If the fee was entirely settled by your primary balance, you’ll see a balance_transaction_id.
  • To see the breakdown of fees relating to a particular product, filter by the feature_name column.

How can I reconcile this report with other Stripe reports?

Reconciliation is subjective and depends on your Stripe account’s configuration. The Fee Report documentation lists the report’s columns and definitions, which you can use to reconcile against other reports.

Balance summary report

You can reconcile the Fees report with the Balance summary report. When reconciling, ensure that each report is generated using the same filters:

  • Both reports must be downloaded for the same date range and time zone.
  • Both reports must have identical account filters (Example: connected account or all connected accounts).
  • For the Fee report, select the “Balance transaction date” filter.
    • The Balance summary report reflects data based on the creation date of the balance transactions.

If you’re looking at the report in itemized format, you can use the Balance transaction ID to match the two reports.

Reconcile fees processed with Stripe Credits with the Balance summary report

The Fees report includes fees processed through the Stripe account balance and Fee Credits. However, the Balance summary report only captures fees that were paid from the Stripe account balance.

Since fees deducted from Stripe Fee Credits don’t impact the Stripe account balance, the “Less fees” value in the “balance change activity” section won’t align with the total fees in the Fees report.

To reconcile the differences, download the Credit Activity report for the specific date and calculate the total amount. The reconciliation can be done using the following formula: Balance Change for Activity Summary “Less Fee” Amount + Fee Credit Amount = Fees Report Amount

Fee Credits

You can reconcile the Fees report with the Credit activity report with this strategy:

Use the Balance transaction ID to match with the Balance summary report and Fee Transaction ID to match with the Credit activity report. The total fees on the Fees report are an aggregation of fees in the Balance summary report and Credit activity report.

Treasury

Not reconcilable, Treasury for platforms reports aren’t supported.

How is the itemized_fees dataset on Stripe Sigma and Data Pipeline different from itemized fees exported on the Dashboard?

The itemized fees exported from the Dashboard may have different available columns from the itemized_fees dataset on Stripe Sigma and Data Pipeline.

Some columns (fee_description, feature_name, product, area) are only available in the Dashboard. Future support for these columns is planned for Stripe Sigma and Data Pipeline.

How to reconcile your qualified tax invoice in Japan

This article will guide you on how to reconcile the fees and taxes displayed on the qualified tax invoices with amounts on your balance report. View sample invoice.

Reconciliation

To verify that the fees and taxes on your qualified tax Invoice match your balance report, follow these steps:

1. Download the qualified tax invoice
  • You can download the qualified tax invoice from the Documents section of your Dashboard (Settings > Plans and fees > Invoice hisotry). The monthly qualified tax invoice is generally available by the 10th of the next month.
2. Download balance report in the Dashboard

  • Go to Reports > Balances

  • Select the Date Range:

  • Make sure to select the month that matches the Service Month of the Qualified Tax Invoice that you are reviewing. The balance report will display data for the prior month by default, which is the right selection if you are reviewing your most recent invoice. You can find the Service Month information on your invoice.

  • Set report time zone: Click the timezone button and select Coordinated Universal Time/UTC to match the timezone used for the qualified tax invoice.

  • Scroll down to Balance change from activity and select Download:

  • Report format: select Itemized

  • Reporting category: select All

  • Columns: select All

  • Follow the prompts to access the downloaded report.

3. Match the amounts in the qualified tax invoice and the balance report

  • To calculate the total fee and tax in the balance report, add the following two amounts:

  • For the lines with reporting_category = ‘fee’, the column ‘gross’ is the amount of fee excluding JCT, and the column ‘fee’ is the amount of JCT; please make sure to exclude JCT tax adjustment described under point 3 below.

  • For the remaining lines in the report (lines with reporting_category different from ‘fee’), use the amount in the ‘fee’ column, which is the fee including any applicable JCT for taxable fees.

  • To match the balance report, sum the total fee and tax from the qualified tax invoice: (Total fees) + (JCT debited from your balance in the ‘current month’)

  • To match the JCT tax adjustment on your qualified tax invoice, download the balance report and select the date range for the month when the JCT tax adjustment was debited or credited to your account (this is shown on your qualified tax invoice). The JCT tax adjustment will be displayed in the balance report as:

  • reporting_category = ‘fee’,

  • column = ‘gross’,

  • description = ‘JCT adjustment for invoice number {invoice number}’

Key notes

  • Invoice-level JCT and transaction-level JCT
    • To comply with the National Tax Agency’s Qualified Invoicing System rounding rules, Stripe will calculate the total JCT when the monthly qualified tax invoice is issued.
    • This is done by calculating and charging JCT at the same time that the respective product fees are charged (“transaction-level JCT”), which may vary by product.
    • At the beginning of the next month when the invoices are issued, JCT is calculated at the invoice-level (“invoice-level JCT”).
    • Where there is a difference between the transaction-level JCT and the invoice-level JCT, Stripe will debit or credit the difference to your account. Because the invoice-level JCT cannot be calculated until after month end, the difference will be debited from or credited to from your account in the month the invoice is issued.
  • Date & Cutoff time for the monthly invoice
    • Stripe issues tax invoices based on the ‘Created’ date in UTC timezone for balance transactions. Balance transactions are changes to your Stripe account balance. You can view your balance transactions via API or by downloading your balance report from the Dashboard.
    • Because tax invoices include balance transactions based on the ‘Created’ date, adjustments to Stripe fees for refunds (also known as “true-ups”) may be included in one month’s tax invoice but refer to payments processed in the previous month.

Check out the articles below to learn more about taxes on Stripe fees in Japan and qualified invoices:

Definition of Terms

Troubleshooting reports with garbled text

When the data has non-English characters (for example, Chinese or Japanese), exported files might have garbled text when opened in Excel or other software. While we are working on to fix the issue, there are some troubleshooting steps you can walk through to try to help fix the problem.

Uploading in Google Sheet

If you have a Google account, Google Sheets can generally safely open reports.

  • Upload the exported file in Google Drive
  • Open the file in Google Sheet and check if there is still garbled text

Changing the text encoding

Windows
  • Open the exported file in Notepad.
  • Go to the File menu; choose “Save As”.
  • Change the Encoding option from UTF-8 to ANSI and save your file.
  • Open the saved file and check if there is still garbled text.
MacOS
  • Open the exported file in TextEdit.
  • Go to the file menu > Duplicate and Save the file.
  • Change Text Encoding option from UTF-8 to UTF-16 or locale code.
  • Open the saved file and check if there is still garbled text.

SEPA Direct Debit

Blocked SEPA debit payments

Stripe helps protect merchants from fraudulent transactions, elevated chargeback rates, and dispute fees by leveraging information collected across our services to detect and block risky transactions. We use both machine learning to detect and block high risk transactions and also use rules to block International Bank Account Numbers (IBAN) based on certain activity.

See How Radar prevents ACH and SEPA Direct Debit payment fraud.

How does Stripe handle suspicious IBANs?

We treat IBANs with more than 3 consecutive disputes or with specific error codes to mitigate fraud risk

If an IBAN has disputed payments 3 times in a row regardless of reason code or at least one dispute for specific reason codes, then we will suspend the IBAN for 90 days, and during this suspension period, future payments using such IBANs will be blocked.

The specific reason codes are:

  • RC01 - Bank identifier incorrect, i.e. invalid BIC
  • AC04 - Account closed
  • AG02 - Invalid bank operation code
  • AC01 - Incorrect account number
  • BE05 - Unrecognised initiating party
  • SL01 - Specific service offered by debtor agent
  • RR02 - Missing debtor name or address

You can find the full list of dispute reason codes on the European Payments Council website.

What will the user see when a payment gets blocked?

When the payment gets blocked you’ll see the error message:

The payment is blocked due to a high likelihood of chargeback.

Why does Stripe block these IBANs?

We have observed that future attempts after these reason codes or attempts that had previous consecutive failures will likely fail again. Blocking such attempts helps improve the chargeback rate and protects your from dispute fees.

Changes to SEPA direct debit address collection

The European Payments Council’s structured address mandate requires city and postal code for SEPA direct debit payment methods when the International Bank Account Numbers (IBAN) is not part of the European Economic Area (EEA).

Do I need to make any changes to my integration?

If you integrate with the API, you’ll need to update your integration before November 15, 2026 to avoid payment failures.

No changes are needed for new transactions on Stripe Checkout, Payment Element, and Hosted Invoices. Stripe automatically surfaces the city and postal code fields as required for SEPA direct debit transactions on these surfaces.

What do I need to update for my API integration?

Update your integration to pass the customer’s billing city in billing details.address.city and postal code in billing details.address.postal_code for SEPA direct debit transactions using non-EEA IBANs. See this list of non-EEA countries.

Do I need to update my customer’s payment method on Stripe?

If you have recurring SEPA direct debit transactions using existing payment methods, you must add the billing_details.postal_code and billing_details.city fields to each payment method before November 15, 2026 to avoid payment failures.

Stripe sent you a list of affected payment methods.

To retrieve a full list of payment methods for your customers, use the List PaymentMethods endpoint.

Update an existing payment method using the API

Use the Update a PaymentMethod endpoint to set billing_details.city and billing_details.postal_code on each payment method.

Detach payment method and collect a new mandate
  • Go to Customers in your Dashboard.
  • Click the customer you want to update.
  • From the Payment Methods section, find and delete the SEPA direct debit payment method.
  • Collect a new payment method from the customer.

Changes to SEPA Direct Debit Payment Behavior

We are changing our payment success timeline for Single Euro Payments Area Direct Debit (SEPA DD) from 2 business days to 6 business days. This change better aligns with the SEPA DD scheme rules and guidelines.

How does the new SEPA DD timeline work?

T+0 is the timestamp when a transaction is initiated. The daily cut off for SEPA DD payments is 10:30 CET. Any payment created after 10:30 CET will be considered as taking place the following business day.

For example, if a payment is initiated at 11:00 CET on Tuesday, March 4th, the payment will succeed on Thursday, March 13th. Since the transaction happened after the cut off, T+0 is Wednesday, March 5th.

  • Wednesday, March 5th (T+0)
  • Thursday, March 6th (T+1)
  • Friday, March 7th (T+2)
  • Monday, March 10th (T+3)
  • Tuesday, March 11th (T+4)
  • Wednesday, March 12th (T+5)
  • Thursday, March 13th (T+6)

The image below shows the previous SEPA DD payment timeline:

The image below shows the updated SEPA DD payment timeline:

Why are we making this change?

The updated timeline will make payment statuses more accurate. Some other benefits include:

  • Improved clarity between failures and disputes: Over 70% of payment failures occurred after payments were prematurely marked as successful and were incorrectly categorized as disputes. By incorporating the recommended five business day waiting period after funds are debited from your customer’s account, we can accurately identify payment failures separate from disputes which are customer-initiated refund requests through their bank.
  • Reduced false positives: Bank-initiated returns such as insufficient funds won’t show a Success state before being marked Disputed. Instead, failures will transition directly to a Failed state. This makes Stripe’s payment success markers more reliable, reduces operational overhead, and prevents fulfillment errors.
  • Reduced double refund fraud: You can only process refunds after payments are marked as successful. We delayed the success status until after the scheme’s failure window, reducing a vulnerability that allowed customers to fraudulently receive refunds. Preventing refunds processing while waiting for failures helps reduce double refund fraud but doesn’t completely remove the problem since customers can still dispute payments in a no-questions-asked 8-week window.

What does the new payment failure timeline look like?

The image below shows the old payment failure timeline. All failures occurring after payment success are categorized as disputes.

The image below shows the new payment failure timeline.

Do you have any tools to help better manage failures?

SEPA DD payments can fail for various reasons, including frozen accounts or insufficient funds. With these changes, you’ll gain improved insights into payment failures through detailed failure codes, enabling better decision-making for recovery actions. Review our guide to effectively manage these situations.

Will these payment success timeline changes break my API integration?

No, the timeline changes won’t affect your API integration.

Are SEPA DD payouts impacted by the new behavior?

The new settlement logic aligns fund availability with payment success, reducing the risk of debiting your external bank account to cover failed payments.

For example, if funds were previously available in your merchant balance on either T+5 or T+7, they will now settle on T+6.

Collecting SEPA Direct Debit mandates from customers

Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) is a payment area within the European Union (EU) that allows banks and payment providers to simplify international payments. A SEPA Direct Debit (SEPA DD) mandate is a legally binding document that allows a business to debit money from a customer’s bank account. A mandate can be used for one-off or recurring payments.

In order to debit an account, businesses must collect their customer’s name and bank account number in International Bank Account Number (IBAN) format. During the payment flow, customers must accept a mandate that gives the business an authorization to debit the account.

Stripe is able to generate this mandate for businesses to present to their customers. See SEPA debit for more information.

What are the benefits of a SEPA DD mandate?

A SEPA DD mandate is a standardized process valid throughout the European Economic Area (EEA) and available in most European countries. Businesses can offer this payment method to their customers if both parties are located in a SEPA payment area.

It simplifies the process of collecting and processing payments. Money can be transferred securely and efficiently using a SEPA DD mandate without delays or problems processing payment transactions.

Businesses can use a mandate to send out automated payment requests and immediately process customer payments. This allows businesses to check the current status of their incoming and outgoing payments at any time.

How does a SEPA DD mandate work?

After signing and submitting a SEPA DD, the customer can automatically pay invoices and direct debits using a credit card or their bank account, or the business can submit direct debits to the customer’s bank using the mandate reference and creditor identifier number. It must be sent to both the recipient and the person sending the money.

Some businesses use preset mandates for regular payment transaction processes, or provide options to improve the payment process for customers. They also need to be transparent when informing customers about collections and give them the opportunity to cancel the mandate at any time. You can find more information on how to issue a SEPA mandate here.

Who signs a SEPA mandate?

A valid SEPA DD mandate must be signed by all parties involved in the transaction. Generally, it needs to be signed by the person acting in the name of the business, which is typically the managing director or another authorized person. If businesses have more than one shareholder, each one will need to receive authorization and provide their signature to ensure that all parties involved in the transaction are fully informed and have given their consent.

If it’s unclear who should sign, businesses should consult their legal advisor about how to proceed.

How long is a SEPA DD mandate valid for?

Once a SEPA DD mandate has been issued, it generally stays valid for 36 months. If the mandate has expired, the business will need to ask their customer to provide consent again in order to keep collecting via SEPA Direct Debits. Mandates can only be extended or renewed in writing and via secure data transfer, like a letter or email.

It’s the company’s responsibility to ensure the mandate is valid. If the mandate is canceled or expires, the business doesn’t have legal means to continue collecting.

What does a SEPA mandate cost?

Usually, there are no fees for customers or businesses unless currency conversion is involved. We recommend asking your principal bank in advance whether they charge fees.

Stripe Apps

Can a Stripe App be translated into my local language?

Stripe Apps are currently only available in English. We’re working on localization tools that will allow app developers to translate their apps into other languages.

Does Stripe review these apps?

Stripe has a review process to ensure that all apps on the marketplace are safe to use and uphold our standards in areas like design, user experience, performance, and reliability. The review process includes a manual review of each app submission as well as automated scans and live testing. Stripe also imposes security and privacy requirements for user data on all apps. Apps are also required to comply with all applicable laws, including data privacy and security laws and regulations. You can see Stripe’s app developer terms here.

To learn more about our review process, please read through the Stripe App Marketplace review requirements.

How can I uninstall an App?

Stripe Apps can be uninstalled by an Administrator from the Installed Apps page.

Click the ellipsis menu for app you want to uninstall and then Uninstall.

How do I build an app for distribution to other businesses?

Once you have developed an app, you can publish it to the Stripe App Marketplace for distribution to other businesses. You can only publish one app per account.

You’ll need to upload your app and then submit it for review. We review your app to make sure it follows the review guidelines.

Once your app has been approved, you can then publish it in the Stripe App Marketplace.

How do I install a Stripe App?

Apps are installed from the Stripe App Marketplace. If you’re an Administrator for your account, you can use the Marketplace to find the listing page for the app you want to install, click the “Install app” button on the top right, and then review the permissions requested by the app developer as well as the app’s privacy policy.

Apps which have UI Extensions will be able available on the right-hand sidebar of your Stripe Dashboard.

Apps are installed only for the Account which is currently active in the Dashboard (of which you must be an Administrator), so if you have multiple accounts, you’ll need to switch the account you’re viewing by clicking on the name of your Stripe account in the upper-left corner and then selecting the account you want to switch to.

How do I make a request for an app?

On the Stripe App Marketplace homepage, you’ll find a “Submit a request” button which will open up your preferred email provider so you can send us your app request.

After you submit your request, we’ll use this feedback to better understand the demand for specific apps or functionalities, so we can ensure that our developers and partners are supplying apps that best meet our users’ needs.

How do I notify Stripe if I have concerns about an app?

Please visit the app settings page where you can use the “Report app to Stripe” button to submit your concerns about an app. We’re available 24/7 to troubleshoot issues for businesses.

How do I report a bug to Stripe regarding the marketplace?

You can let us know about any potential bugs via the contact form on the right-hand sidebar of this support page. Please select “Other” as the topic and in your message provide a detailed report of the issue as well as what page it is on. We’re available 24/7 to troubleshoot issues for businesses.

How do I submit an app for review, and what does the review entail?

To submit an app for review, follow the steps listed here and read through the app listing guidelines and review guidelines to ensure that you are meeting all of the required criteria.

To help us complete our review as quickly as possible, it’s important that all of your information is accurate before you submit your app for approval. If you make changes after submitting your app, we’ll need to restart the review process.

Once you’ve completed your submission, we’ll review your app to make sure it meets all of the review guidelines.

If approved, you can make your app available in the Stripe App Marketplace. Otherwise, we’ll send you feedback on areas where your app did not meet the requirements for approval.

How do I update an extension to a Stripe App?

A Stripe extension allowed users to sync Stripe data to other business tools, like analytics dashboards, data warehouses, or other 3rd party services. In July of 2022 we launched Stripe Apps, a new way for you to integrate all the tools you use to run your business.

All legacy extensions will be deprecated by 2024. To guarantee continued functionality it is best to update to a Stripe App whenever possible. A complete list of available apps can be found in the Stripe App Marketplace.

If you are already using an extension, those with an available Stripe App can be viewed and upgraded to in the App Settings page in the Stripe Dashboard.

Update to a Stripe App

To complete an upgrade from the App Settings page an Administrator can select “Update” next to the desired Stripe App.

Upon choosing to Update, you’ll be prompted to accept permissions. After reviewing and accepting the new permissions, the Stripe App will be installed.

After successfully installing the new Stripe App, you’ll find your new app in the Stripe Apps drawer located on the right side of your dashboard.

Depending on the Stripe App, you may have additional onboarding to complete in the app or the app provider’s service external site.

In-App Subscriptions

Stripe Apps has an integration with a third party app provider Revenue Cat to help you implement and manage in-app subscriptions.

RevenueCat is a subscription platform for mobile apps. It allows developers to easily deploy cross-platform subscriptions, manage products and subscribers, and analyze customer data. The RevenueCat Stripe App combines Stripe’s standard customer data and enriches it using RevenueCat’s SDKs and subscription backend into a single page view.

Stripe Apps allow you to connect Stripe with your help desk, accounting software, and more so that you can simplify workflows and add context in Stripe to give you a holistic view of your business.

If you’re interested in integrations that can help you do more with Stripe, contact our partnerships team.

What is e-invoicing?

The Stripe App Marketplace offers multiple e-invoicing providers like Billit and Pennylane, that work directly with your Stripe Invoicing flow.

What is e-invoicing?

Electronic invoicing, or e-invoicing, means sending or receiving invoices in a standardized, machine-readable electronic format as opposed to unstructured formats such as email-delivered PDFs or paper invoices.

Requirements for the specific e-invoicing format (such as XML, JSON, or UBL) and the transmission network (such as the global PEPPOL network or SDI in Italy) vary from country to country.

Incorporating e-invoicing into billing processes is increasingly common as it allows for more systematic and consistent tracking of invoices across buyers and sellers.

How do I know if my business needs e-invoicing?

E-invoicing is also mandated for certain types of transactions in an effort to increase tax compliance. Countries that require e-invoices include France, Italy, and Germany in Europe, and Mexico and Brazil in Latin America.

For certain regions with e-invoicing mandates, there may also be additional requirements to report e-invoice data to the tax administration (“e-reporting” or “real-time reporting”).

The requirement to use e-invoicing is often limited to specific transaction types (B2B), verticals (government buyers), or cross-border status (domestic sales only).

Consult with your tax or legal advisor to determine whether and which e-invoicing and e-reporting requirements apply to your business per the latest rules and regulations.

How do I incorporate e-invoicing into my business?

For Stripe Billing and Invoicing users, the Stripe App Marketplace offers multiple e-invoicing providers (e.g. Billit) that are compatible with your invoicing workflow.

When evaluating your e-invoicing provider, check to make sure they comply with e-invoicing standards in the countries you operate in. After finding a provider that suits your needs in the Stripe App Marketplace, download the app and follow onboarding steps to connect e-invoicing to your current Stripe Billing/Invoicing flow.

Where do I go to use a Stripe App?

Where your app appears in the Dashboard depends on the type of app.

Drawer apps are available in the app dock in the upper-right corner of the Dashboard. Click an app icon to open it in a drawer. What the drawer shows can depend on which Dashboard page you have open. For example, an app that displays customer information only appears when you’re viewing a customer details page.

Full-page apps appear in the Apps section of the left navigation. Click an app to open a dedicated full-page experience within the Dashboard. You can also find full-page apps using Dashboard search.

API-only apps don’t have a graphical interface and grant access to your Stripe data to the app vendor upon your permission. They’re active from the moment they’re installed and set-up.

You can manage all your installed apps from Apps > Apps overview > Installed.

Who can use Stripe Apps on my account?

Once you install an app on your account, any user on your team will be immediately able to see it and use it. However, only Administrators can change app settings or uninstall an app.

In the future, we may add the ability for Administrators to also restrict which users or roles can use specific apps.

Why can’t I install an App?

If the Install app button on an app listing page is disabled, this can be due to any of the following reasons.

You are not logged in to Stripe

You need to be logged in to install an app. Log in before returning to the Marketplace listing.

You are not an Administrator for your account

Only team members with the Administrator role can install, uninstall, and manage apps for an account. To check if you’re an Administrator for any of your accounts, go to your personal details and scroll down to the Accounts section to see your role in each account.

Stripe Apps are not supported by your Platform

If your account is connected to a Platform – that is, a third-party that administers payments and data on your account – they may not support app installation for connected accounts.

You can find out if your account is connected to a Platform by following these steps.

You are the developer of the app

You cannot install an app on the account that has published it through the Marketplace. The app will already be installed on your account through the upload process. If you wish to test installation of an app you’ve published, you can create a new account.

Stripe Sigma

Can I use Stripe Sigma in test mode to schedule a queried run?

Stripe Sigma only runs on livemode data. It’s not possible to test scheduled query Stripe Sigma runs in test mode.

My Stripe Sigma query with map lookup has stopped working

Error Message: “INVALID_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT: Key not present in map”

Resolution: Use ELEMENT_AT() instead of [] for map lookup.

For example, if your query looks like:

SELECT charge_id, metadata[‘customer’] FROM (
  SELECT charge_id, map_agg(key, value) AS metadata FROM charges_metadata
)

Change it to:

SELECT charge_id, ELEMENT_AT(metadata, 'customer') FROM (
  SELECT charge_id, map_agg(key, value) AS metadata FROM charges_metadata
)

Additional Information

As of September 3rd 2020, Stripe Sigma supports queries using Prestosql v334 SQL syntax. As a part of this change, map lookup with [] will fail if the key is not present in the map. ELEMENT_AT()resumes the previous behavior of returning NULL for key absence.

Scheduled and saved queries have been updated accordingly.

Why has the capitalization of column header in my Stripe Sigma query result changed?

As of September 3rd 2020, Stripe Sigma supports queries using Prestosql v334 SQL syntax. As a part of this change, capitalization of column header is preserved from original column name in subqueries.

For example:

SELECT * FROM ( SELECT AmoUnT FROM charges )

Old behavior:

amount
1.23

New behavior:

AmoUnT
1.23

Why has the format of object value in my Stripe Sigma query result changed?

As of September 3rd 2020, Stripe Sigma supports queries using Prestosql v334 SQL syntax. As a part of this change, object values, such as map and array, are now encoded in JSON format.

For example:

SELECT id, map_agg(key, value) AS dictionary FROM charges_metadata GROUP BY id

Old behavior:

id, dictionary
ch_123,{a=123, b=hello world}
...

New behavior:

id, dictionary
ch_123,"{""a"":""123"",""b"":""hello world""}"

Stripe Tax

Charging sales tax, GST, or VAT on payments

Sales and other indirect tax requirements vary by region, so we recommend checking with a qualified accountant to understand your business’s setup and any required taxes you should be including in your charges.

Including taxes in charges

There are two ways to charge your customers sales tax, VAT, or GST.

  • Stripe Tax - Stripe Tax automatically calculates and collects the right amount of tax depending on the tax code you select and your customer’s location. You can see where you need to register to collect taxes based on your transaction history, have the ability to choose whether tax is applied inclusively or exclusively, and can access reports to see how much tax you have collected in a given jurisdiction.
  • Dynamic Tax Rates - With Dynamic Tax Rates, you can manually create your own log of tax rates and apply them to your customers’ invoices or checkout sessions. Similarly you can set the rate of tax to be charged inclusively or exclusively. With Tax Rates, Stripe does not calculate relevant taxes for you, and you maintain your log of applicable tax codes and rates. As with Stripe Tax, you are able to export reports of how much tax you have collected.

Does Stripe Tax work with Payment Links?

Stripe Tax is supported with Payment Links, along with Billing, Invoices, and Checkout. If you want to enable Stripe Tax on these transactions, you can add one line of code or enable the ‘automatic tax’ toggle in tax settings. You can also use Stripe Tax on custom payment flows with the Orders API

Additional Information

Payment Links Stripe Tax What Countries is Stripe Tax Available in?

Information on why negative tax amounts may appear on your location reports

Stripe Tax’s location reports will report refunds and other negative adjustments in the period in which they occur. Sometimes there are not enough sales in the location in the current period to offset the refunds or other negative amounts that occur in the same period. This causes the location report to have a net negative total balance for the period.

Let’s walk through an example: One of your customers purchases an item and pays $25 of tax on that order in January. This $25 of tax is included on your January return (filed in February) and is remitted to the state. That same customer then returns that item in April and you now have “negative” $25 of tax applied to the April period. However, you don’t have any sales in this particular location in April, so your report reflects a negative $25 of tax at the close of the April period.

Some states allow taxpayers to report negative subtotals on the return. However, many do not and this can cause issues when you file your return. For this reason, we recommend that you reach out to the taxing authority or a sales tax expert for guidance on how to accurately file your returns and reclaim any tax previously remitted to the state.

Manage draft subscription invoices with invalid tax location details

Automatic tax with Stripe Billing relies on a customer’s location to determine the correct tax rate. If a customer’s address, payment method’s address, or default payment method is changed or missing, Stripe Tax may not be able to determine a valid tax rate.

When Stripe Tax can’t determine a tax rate, the subscription invoices stay in “draft” status until you resolve the issue which means subscriptions remain active and payment is not collected, so you may be providing services to these customers without receiving payment.

You were notified via webhook and email when your first subscription invoice failed to finalize. On November 25, 2024, Stripe is improving product behavior and automatic guardrails to prevent similar issues in the future.

Identifying and exporting unpaid invoices

Follow the below steps to 1) identify subscriptions and invoices that failed to finalize, 2) find the reason for their failure, and 3) export this information as a CSV file. You can use the Stripe Dashboard or the Invoicing API.

Identifying invoices that failed to finalize due to invalid customer tax location
  • This pre-filtered link will take you to the relevant invoices. Results are filtered by Frequency: Subscription invoice and Automatic tax: Enabled to help you focus on automatic tax enabled subscription invoices.
  • Click Export.
  • Select columns Last Finalization Error Code and any others you’re interested in.
  • Export.
  • Filter results by Last Finalization Error Code = customer_tax_location_invalid.
Identifying subscriptions with invalid customer tax location
  • This pre-filtered link will take you to the relevant subscriptions. Results are filtered by Automatic tax: Enabled to help you focus on automatic tax enabled subscriptions only.
  • Click Export.
  • Choose “Custom” in the columns drop down and select Tax Location Recognized and any others you’re interested in.
  • Export.
  • Filter results by Tax Location Recognized = false.

What are my options for previous draft, unpaid invoices?

You can address the draft invoices you identified in two ways depending on the specific error: whether the invoice requires an updated address or is missing a default payment method. Identify the underlying issue and based on your business need, choose one or more of the solutions described below.

Solution 1: Reattempt collection

Reattempt payment collection on each invoice with automatic tax by adding the missing details. Alternatively, disable automatic tax before finalizing the invoice.

Before proceeding with any of the below steps, we recommend confirming with the impacted customers that they still intend to subscribe to your service. Failure to do so could result in chargebacks. To try collecting payment:

  • Verify there’s a valid payment method for your customer if your invoice is set to charge automatically. If the default payment method is missing, contact your customer to add one.
  • If your invoice is configured to send an email instead of charging automatically, skip this step.
  • Collect a customer location, or proceed without taxes.

(Option A) Collect a valid location for the customer: Update the customer’s address using one of:

  • The Customer Update API.
  • The Stripe Dashboard
  • Sending a Customer Portal link to your customers. To provide a link that goes directly to where your customer can update their billing details, add /customer/update to the end of the session URL. This will look like: billing.stripe.com>/customer/update

(Option B) Collect without tax

  • Turn off Stripe Tax. Use the update invoice API or invoice editor in the Dashboard to disable automatic tax on the invoice.
  • Finalize and then pay or send the invoice to collect payment. Use the Dashboard to finalize and then either send or process payment on the invoice depending on your business’s collection method. Alternatively, use the finalize API as well as either the send or pay API.
  • Resume collection on the Subscription.

⚠️ When finalizing the invoice without automatic tax, keep in mind that tax will not be calculated or collected on that invoice. You’ll need to manage any related tax responsibilities. We recommend connecting with your tax advisor for guidance.

Solution 2: Cancel subscriptions (recommended when payment details can’t be collected)

If services weren’t provided or if collecting payment is not feasible, cancel the subscription by navigating to the subscription in your Stripe account. It’s not possible to void or delete draft subscription invoices so no further action is required.

What is Stripe doing to prevent future invoices from being stuck in draft?

Prevent invalid updates to customer locations

Effective Date: Starting Nov 25, 2024

Our Customer Update API now prevents customers from updating their addresses to invalid locations when they have subscriptions with automatic tax enabled. For invalid addresses, the API returns an HTTP 400 error with the code customer_tax_location_invalid. As before, the Customer Portal validates addresses entered by your customers to ensure they are valid for Stripe Tax.

Disable automatic tax when auto-finalizing invoices with invalid locations

Effective Date: Starting Nov 25, 2024

When a subscription renews automatically, we’ll attempt to calculate tax and finalize the invoice. If tax calculation fails because the customer location is invalid, then automatic tax calculation will be disabled on the invoice and its subscription.

In this scenario, the invoice will be finalized without calculating or collecting tax, rather than remaining in a “draft” status. This change allows you to collect payment even when tax can’t be calculated. You’ll receive events for this change, such as invoice.updated and customer.subscription.updated, showing that automatic tax has been turned off. These allow you to take action on invoices and subscriptions that are missing valid location inputs and re-enable automatic tax for future payments. The automatic_tax[disabled_reason] field will be set to finalization_requires_location_inputs on this invoice. In the case of a missing payment method, the invoice will finalize and payment failures will be retried according to Stripe’s standard retry and recovery processes. After reaching the maximum number of attempts, the subscription may transition to a past_due or canceled status, depending on your Billing settings.

This change does not apply when finalizing an invoice via the Stripe API or Dashboard. In those cases, automatic tax stays enabled if the customer location is missing or not valid, and the finalization fails with a HTTP 400 error.

To review subscriptions without automatic tax calculations in your Stripe Dashboard, visit your Subscriptions page and filter the view by the Automatic tax not enabled option.

To reactivate automatic tax for these subscriptions in the future, ensure that there is at least one valid customer location available. You can then activate automatic tax through the Stripe Tax dashboard.

Tax liability for past invoices

Sales tax, VAT, or GST can’t be retroactively enabled for past invoices. As a merchant, you remain liable for any applicable taxes on sales made prior to the implementation of any tax settings. It is essential to ensure compliance with tax regulations moving forward, and we recommend consulting with a tax advisor to understand your obligations regarding previous transactions. If you have any further questions or need assistance, reach out to our support team.

Understanding Stripe Tax pricing

Stripe Tax offers two plans:

  • Tax Complete offers tax registrations, calculations, collections, and filings, and is priced as a monthly subscription with a 1-year contract.
  • Tax Basic offers tax calculations and collections only, and is priced on a pay-as-you-go basis.

Fees for Stripe Tax are automatically deducted from your Stripe Balance, and are based on the location of the merchant, regardless of where the transaction takes place. For example, a merchant based in the US, selling products to various countries, will be charged in USD. While the prices in this article are listed in USD, a merchant will be charged an equivalent amount in their local currency.

Tax Complete: Subscription-based pricing

This is an annual contract, paid monthly. The option to sign up for Tax Complete is only available if it’s supported in your region. If eligible, sign up or switch to a subscription-based plan from the Your plans page in the Stripe Dashboard. The monthly subscription fee is deducted from your Stripe Balance at the start of each billing period. Any overage fees, and additional fees for registrations and filings outside of the US, are deducted after the billing period ends.

Tax Complete offers four pricing tiers. Each tier includes a set number of tax registrations, transactions, calculations, and filings. Overage fees may apply if you exceed these limits.

Tax Basic: Pay-as-you-go (PAYG) pricing

PAYG pricing is usage-based and determined by the number of transactions or the sales volume that you process through Stripe Tax for tax calculation and collection. You only incur fees for transactions in jurisdictions where you have an active tax registration. The pricing differs based on the type of integration you use (no-code vs API).

PAYG no-code integration with Stripe Billing, Invoicing, Checkout, and Payment Links

PAYG pricing for Stripe Tax no-code integration is 0.5% of the volume processed, in jurisdictions where you are registered to collect tax. This volume includes the complete transaction amount, including any calculated sales tax.

PAYG Stripe Tax API pricing

Stripe Tax provides two distinct APIs: Calculations API and Transactions API. Both APIs are priced based on the number of API calls you make.

  • Transaction API price per call: 0.50 USD
  • Calculation API price per call: 0.05 USD

Fees for the API are specific to each market and based on the location of the merchant, regardless of where the transaction takes place. For example, a merchant based in the US, selling products to various countries, is charged in USD for all transactions.

Stripe Tax Calculations API only

You’ll be charged from your Stripe Balance on a daily basis for all Calculation API calls made.

Stripe Tax Calculations and Transactions APIs

With every Transaction API call, you receive up to 10 Calculation API calls for free. If you exceed the 10 Calculation API calls per Transaction API call, 0.05 USD is charged per additional Calculation call. This is aggregated on a monthly basis.

Stripe Tax API customers are charged on a daily basis for all Calculation and Transaction API calls made. At the end of each calendar month, a rebate is applied if there’s a difference in Calculation API calls. Rebates are typically completed by the end of the month, followed by an additional three business days. Unused Calculation API calls don’t carry over to the next month.

FAQ

Is the Stripe Tax Transaction API call the same as a payment transaction?

No, the Stripe Tax Transaction API call is independent from a successful payments transaction. You need to call the Transaction API specifically for Stripe Tax. This is consistent for all Stripe API products.

Can I use Registrations and Filings if I’m on a custom pricing plan?

Yes, users on a custom pricing plan for tax calculations can purchase registrations and filings directly in the Dashboard. You’ll be charged the overage rates mentioned above. Custom pricing is available for companies with large payments volume, high-value transactions, or unique business models.

Related articles

Stripe tax fee use cases

What happens to the funds after tax is collected on Stripe?

When using Stripe Tax or Tax Rates, once the respective amount of tax has been collected from your customer, it will be added to your Stripe account balance and then paid out to you accordingly as per your payout preferences. If you’re a business collecting taxes, you must report, file, and remit the taxes collected in every jurisdiction that you’re registered in.

You can use the tax reports from the Dashboard to help understand how much tax you might have collected in a jurisdiction and are required to remit.

Please ensure you understand and comply with obligations of each jurisdiction and consult your tax advisor if you need help.

Strong Customer Authentication

Businesses affected by Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) regulations

Europe

All European Economic Area (EEA)-based businesses charging cards online that were also issued in the EEA are required to comply with SCA and could see increased declines if their Stripe checkout process does not include an authentication step as required by SCA rules, which is available via Stripe Checkout or the Payment Intents API.

UK

The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has released guidance that in the event of a no-deal Brexit, SCA enforcement will be implemented as planned. See our Q&A on Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) enforcement date for the most current details on timing.

US and Other Countries

Businesses based outside the EEA are considered out of scope of and should see minimal impact due to SCA. Transactions generated from businesses outside of the EEA are considered a one-leg transactions and therefore not subject to SCA rules.

  • Some European card issuers might choose to decline one-leg transactions, but based on recent discussions with banks in Europe, we expect that this will be uncommon.
  • If you are concerned about declines on one-leg transactions, you can consider integrating Stripe Checkout or the Payment Intents API to prepare. If you are using 3D Secure (3DS) on Sources, you can update your logic to require authentication for EU-based cardholders.
  • While requiring an authentication step can potentially introduce friction that might end in incomplete/lost sales, if you upgrade to Stripe Checkout or the Payment Intents API, you can take advantage of 3D Secure 2 which introduces frictionless authentication that is not available/possible with 3D Secure using Sources.

Additional Information

  • If you are a Connect platform not in the EEA, see: Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) for Destination Charges Created by Non-European Economic Area (EEA) Platform for EEA-Based Connected Account and EEA-Based Customer
  • United Kingdom and Brexit: Stripe expects that SCA will still apply to UK-based business and cardholders even in the event of a no-deal Brexit when the UK FCA begins enforcing SCA in September 2021. Additionally, UK merchants are already seeing declines from partial enforcement in other EEA countries
  • Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) Dashboard, Preparation, and Resources

Countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) impacted by Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) regulation

As of 2020-08-17, the following countries are considered part of the European Economic Area (EEA) and in scope of Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) regulation:

  • Austria = AT
  • Belgium = BE
  • Bulgaria = BG
  • Croatia = HR
  • Cyprus = CY
  • Czech Republic = CZ
  • Denmark = DK

Create a client-side subscription without Checkout session

This can be done using the Stripe API:

  • Create a payment method.
  • Attach the payment method to the customer.
  • Create the subscription using default_payment_method.
  • Alternatively, update the customer object with invoice_settings[default_payment_method] to set the payment method to the default for all invoices and subscriptions, then create the subscription.

Identify if your Stripe account is connected to partner solutions

You can see which third-party applications have been granted access to your Stripe account by visiting your Settings and clicking on Authorized applications. Applications shown, such as third-party plugins or platforms, are considered partner solutions.

Received Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) email for unused Stripe account

If you no longer process charges through a Stripe account that has received an email about Strong Customer Authentication (SCA), no action is necessary. If you have another active Stripe account and you are located in the European Economic Area (EEA), charges created through that account will be subject to SCA regulation and updates to your integration are necessary.

If you are unsure which Stripe account the email applies to, you can click on the Visit the Dashboard link in the email, and it will redirect to the impacted Stripe account.

Multiple recommendations

  • If you have multiple charge flows, you might receive multiple recommendations.
  • Depending on how you want to accept payments, using separate options like Stripe Billing for your recurring charges or Stripe Checkout for purchases while your customers are online are available. If you are looking for a solution that fits all charge flows, transitioning to the Payment Intents API is recommended.

Stripe Connect compliance under PSD2

Stripe Connect is compliant with Payment Services Directive 2 (PSD2). For more details, you can read our guide to Strong Customer Authentication (SCA).

Strong Customer Authentication

As of 14 September 2019, new authentication requirements are being introduced for online payments in Europe as part of the second Payments Services Directive (PSD2). Payments where both the business and the customer’s bank are located in the European Economic Area (EEA) need to meet the new Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) requirements. This means adding an extra layer of security for customers making purchases online. Businesses with European Stripe accounts charging European customers may need to update their Stripe integration to support the additional authentication requirements. Find more about SCA below, or view our Strong Customer Authentication guide in the Stripe Docs.

Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) integration recommendation questionnaire

To determine how you should update your integration to be SCA-ready:

  • Visit your SCA dashboard.
  • Click Get Started to complete the integration questionnaire
  • Click on View Recommendations to see suggestions for SCA preparation tailored to your integration.

Additional Information

  • If you do not see the Get Started button, see “Get Started” Button Not Showing in Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) Dashboard for the Integration Questionnaire.
  • You can re-take the questionnaire from the SCA dashboard.

WooCommerce plug-in and Strong Customer Authentication support

The latest version of the Stripe plugin for WooCommerce, version 4.3.0, is Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) ready. This version supports SCA for recurring charges and subscriptions.
